{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Canonical slugs to prefer: `anthropic`, `openai`, `google-deepmind`, `meta`, `xai`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `qwen`, `nvidia`, `microsoft`, `amazon`, `apple`, `threat-intel`, `cyber-offense`, `cyber-defense`, `influence-ops`, `scams-fraud`, `deepfakes`, `prompt-injection`, `agents`, `agent-security`, `alignment`, `interpretability`, `evals`, `open-weights`, `reasoning-models`, `scaling`, `compute`, `chips`, `export-controls`, `energy`, `datacenters`, `china`, `eu-ai-act`, `us-federal-policy`, `us-state-policy`, `uk`, `copyright`, `privacy`, `military`, `autonomous-weapons`, `pentagon`, `healthcare`, `fda`, `drug-discovery`, `bio-risk`, `ai-for-science`, `robotics`, `labor`, `education`, `elections`, `surveillance`, `child-safety`, `incidents`, `funding`, `earnings`. Add an entity slug (company, agency, named group) when the story is about that entity.

**Storylines** (optional; usually one, at most two): the ids from `node scripts/build.js --storylines` whose arc this item advances — a new development in *that story*, not merely the same topic. Only existing ids with status `live` or `proposed`; the validator rejects unknown or resolved ids. Omit the key when the item belongs to none. Never coin an id here.

results:
I didn't find a bill that would require federal permission to train advanced AI models. The closest matches are draft proposals, and none appears to have passed.

- **Great American AI Act (draft):** This 269-page draft would bar states from regulating how models are developed for three years, while leaving deployment and use open to state rules. It comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models. The bill would preempt state laws and regulation "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. It also has mandatory disclosure and risk-mitigation requirements for frontier models.
- **Frontier-developer scope:** The bill would apply to "frontier developers," defined as entities that train, or initiate the training of, a frontier model using more than 10^26 integer or floating point operations. That threshold is a compute trigger, not a permit requirement.
- **FRONTIER Act:** Reps. Lori Trahan and Jay Obernolte advanced the FRONTIER Act, which would authorize government intervention against risky models and override some state laws.
- **Blackburn's draft ("Trump America AI Act"):** It would require certain developers to participate in evaluation programs and submit advanced systems to the Department of Energy for testing and oversight, according to the draft.
- **Hawley-Blumenthal bill:** This would prohibit the use of personally identifiable or copyrighted data to train AI models without consent.

The results contain nothing dated November 2026, and the newest items are from July 2026, so I couldn't confirm the current status of any of these. Some of the sources also describe these bills as drafts still in feedback, so it's worth checking Congress.gov for introduced versions before relying on any of this.

# Hackers use AntiFox AI agents in AWS credential-theft attacks

By

# Bill Toulas

- November 11, 2026

- 10:12 AM

- 0



Attackers are using Alibaba Cloud to host self-managed instances of AntiFox, an open-source agentic penetration testing platform, to target web services and AWS environments.



The infrastructure hosting AntiFox was used for various malicious activities, including vulnerability exploitation, webshell deployment, credential validation, configuration discovery, and AWS secret harvesting.



Initially created as a fork of ARTEX 0.1.1, AntiFox has a Chinese-language interface and lets users deploy AI agents and automate common penetration-testing tasks, such as mapping exposed services and probing target endpoints for vulnerabilities.



Security researchers at Arctic Wolf observed malicious AntiFox-linked infrastructure hosted on Alibaba Cloud using valid AWS identities, including IAM users and, in some cases, assumed EC2 roles, to make authenticated requests to Amazon Web Services APIs.



“In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments,” Arctic Wolf says .



One case highlighted in the report involved deploying an ASPX webshell on an internet-exposed IIS server, executing OS commands, accessing application settings and database connection strings, and copying configuration and log files to a web-accessible directory.



The attacker also used valid IAM credentials and EC2 roles to probe Amazon Web Services (AWS) endpoints. In one intrusion, they cycled through multiple identities and made hundreds of API requests in about 30 minutes, the researchers note.



Although most of these attempts were blocked, the attacker was successful in some cases and obtained production secrets.



In a separate incident, the attackers used a valid AWS identity to read, copy, and delete S3 objects.



Arctic Wolf's report includes hunting guidance and recommendations for defenders that include correlating IIS webshell activity with unusual AWS access and reviewing successful API calls within bursts of denials.



The researchers also recommend revoking affected AWS sessions and keys and rotating credentials exposed through application files.



The AntiFox findings follow recent attacks involving ARTEX AI, another agentic penetration-testing framework developed in China that went closed-source after it was used in attacks on South Korean banks .



CrowdStrike also linked ARTEX to a cyberespionage campaign in which the Chinese hacking group Vapor Panda targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries.



For now, AntiFox remains available on GitHub, where it has been updated to version 2.0, which improves how the tool documents and reports findings.



Its publishers prohibit using the tool against live systems, in real-world penetration tests or security exercises, or for destructive or illegal activity, but they do not describe any technical controls that enforce those restrictions.



Update 12/11 - An Amazon spokesperson sent BleepingComputer the following statement about the above:



"AWS services were not compromised and operated as designed. The research describes threat actors using credentials taken from customers’ compromised applications to access their AWS accounts. As always, we recommend all customers follow security, identity, and compliance best practices, including granting least-privilege permissions, requiring IMDSv2 on EC2 instances, keeping long-term access keys out of application configurations, and turning on Amazon GuardDuty. Customers who suspect unauthorized activity in their accounts should follow guidance for remediating potentially compromised credentials or contact AWS Support." - Amazon spokesperson

# Notion says Fireworks breach exposed customer AI chat transcripts

By

# Bill Toulas

- November 11, 2026

- 03:54 PM

- 0



Notion, the digital workspace platform, disclosed that a security breach at its AI infrastructure provider, Fireworks AI, exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces.



The disclosure comes shortly after Fireworks AI confirmed that an attacker accessed its development environment via a third-party cloud provider on October 23 and compromised resource metadata, billing information, model weights, and datasets for some customers.



Fireworks AI experienced another breach in early October, when hackers accessed environment variables containing API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts.



Notion learned about the exposed chat transcripts after receiving an alert from Fireworks on November 2 about an exposed dataset that contained only synthetic test data.



Notion responded by cutting off traffic to Fireworks, deleting all data from the vendor’s systems, and halting training runs by November 3.



However, Fireworks confirmed on November 8 that customer data had been accessed, including that of Notion users .



Notion is a cloud-based workspace used for note-taking, document creation, internal wikis, project management, and task tracking. It includes an AI assistant that can answer questions, summarize content, and help draft text.



Fireworks AI enables Notion to run some of the open-weight models available through Notion AI and analyze stored conversations for Insights, a feature that gives workspace administrators visibility into how their teams use AI.



The exposed transcripts came from the Insights dataset specifically, which has now been disabled.



“Upon analysis of the dataset Fireworks AI gave us on November 8, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable,” Notion stated in an update .



"Unattributable means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results.”



Notion has also published a FAQ page about the incident, highlighting that Fireworks had contractually committed to zero data retention for Notion data.



According to the company, less than 1% of its users are impacted by the incident. Potentially affected workspace owners should review the data through Security incident review in Notion’s desktop web interface and share a link with members that lets them download their own transcripts.



Notion advises affected users to rotate any passwords, API keys, or other credentials entered into affected chats.



If neither a user nor their workspace owner has received a notice, Notion says no action is needed for now, and they are most likely not part of the impacted subset.

Title:
Auditable Human-Agent Teams for Autonomous X-ray Experimentation

Gunik Luthra , Ronald J. Pandolfi , Benjamin T. Diroll , Ricky Ronquillo , Ruipeng Li , Christopher B. Murray , Marcus M. Noack , Kevin G. Yager , Esther H. R. Tsai

Subjects:
Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)

Closed-loop autonomous experimentation can accelerate scientific discovery, but implementation effort limits accessibility. Agentic systems may lower this barrier, although sustained operation on physical instruments remains largely unexplored. Here, using coding-agent infrastructure grounded in validated scientific methods, we demonstrate autonomous synchrotron X-ray experiments on nanoparticle superlattices under evolving, human-defined objectives. Complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts enable an audit that reconstructs decision provenance and characterizes the division of cognitive labor. Across three experiments, 61-67% of messages involved interpretation or judgment, while the share of methodological and scientific contributions increased from 46% in the setup-focused first experiment to 56-61% in later experiments. Provenance showed that 59-68% of error corrections involved multiple participants and that about half of all decisions incorporated the input of another participant. These results may guide design principles for multi-agent scientific systems and inform future agent harnesses, model training, and accessible autonomous experimentation.

-0500 Keep US troops in NATO’s KFOR https://www.defenseone.com/ideas/2026/11/keep-us-troops-natos-kfor/417171/ Pulling them out would save almost nothing while handing Moscow a cheap strategic win. Ivana Stradner and Mark Montgomery Wed, 11 Nov 2026 16:04:13 -0500 https://www.defenseone.com/ideas/2026/11/keep-us-troops-natos-kfor/417171/ Ideas As the Pentagon finalizes its review of U.S. force posture in Europe, one relatively small commitment deserves protection from the budget axe: the roughly 600 American troops serving in NATO’s Kosovo Force. They barely register in a debate about brigades and billion-dollar line items, but they keep a hard-won peace in the Balkans, and pulling them out would save almost nothing while handing Moscow a cheap strategic win.

KFOR was deployed in June 1999 under NATO command, after the alliance bombed Yugoslavia to stop the violence perpetrated by Slobodan Milosevic’s Serbian forces against ethnic Albanians. Kosovo declared independence in 2008, but Serbia, backed by Russia and China, still refuses to recognize it.

The Europe posture review is a legitimate exercise. After years of urging European allies to shoulder more of their own conventional defense, the Trump administration is right to ask hard questions about where American forces add unique value and where Europe can step up given suitable time to develop their capabilities and capacities. But KFOR is a mission in which the American role is not easily replaced, because it is as much political as military, and where a wrong call risks instability on Europe’s southeastern flank.

Start with the threat. Even while absorbing heavy losses in Ukraine, Vladimir Putin has not given up on destabilizing Europe. The Balkans, Europe’s soft underbelly, are a favored arena: cheap to stir, a place to distract Western attention from Ukraine. Moscow has long used Serbia as a lever against Kosovo’s stability. In 2017, a Russian-made train was sent toward northern Kosovo, a rolling provocation that bore the slogan “Kosovo is Serbia.” Russia runs a so-called humanitarian center near Kosovo that is suspected of serving as a Russian intelligence station. Close Serbian-Russian intelligence ties give Moscow access to local nationalist forces prepared for provocations. In 2023, an armed attack on Kosovo police in the north, which Pristina blamed on Serbian-backed militants, heightened fears that Russian-aligned actors were exploiting the tension; earlier that year, Russia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs warned that “a major explosive situation is brewing in the heart of Europe.”

Tensions have repeatedly flared. In May 2023, clashes between Serb protesters and Kosovo police injured more than 90 NATO peacekeepers and prompted Serbia to raise its military alert level. That September, an attack in Banjska, where heavily armed Serb gunmen killed a Kosovo police officer and barricaded themselves in a monastery, showed how quickly a local flare-up can become a regional crisis.

The danger has not passed. Serbian strongman Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Serbia’s Oct. 25 parliamentary election, but Belgrade’s foreign-policy direction is uncertain and there are concerns that its views on Kosovo will not change. In October, Russia’s ambassador to the UN warned that the situation in Kosovo “remains persistently tense and is literally teetering on the brink.”

Still, Kosovo and Serbia have remained at peace since 1999, in large part because of KFOR. In the words of a bipartisan group of U.S lawmakers, the force functions as “a political deterrent to those seeking to stoke ethnic violence.” An American drawdown from KFOR may embolden nationalist agendas in Kosovo and Serbia as well as separatist ambitions in Republika Srpska, the Serb-dominated region in nearby Bosnia.

The American presence in KFOR is valued precisely because it is American. U.S. troops have anchored KFOR since its creation, and Washington currently leads Regional Command East, a position of real operational weight, not symbolism. The U.S. has traditionally provided the 600 or so American troops—often Army National Guardsmen—an economy-of-force mission with minimal cost or effect on the U.S. Army’s ability to execute missions elsewhere around the globe. The mission accounts for less than 1 percent of the total U.S. troops in Europe.

KFOR’s value becomes plain when contrasted with Operation Althea in neighboring Bosnia. EUFOR, an EU-led force with roughly 1,500 troops, has struggled to respond decisively to repeated provocations by Republika Srpska leader Milorad Dodik, who’s backed by Moscow and Belgrade. EU ambassadors rejected Bosnian appeals to help enforce an arrest warrant against him in 2025, citing political risk. Dodik has openly mocked EUFOR’s patrols. Lacking an American anchor and a unified chain of command willing to act, EUFOR has too often had to manage crises rather than deterring them.

KFOR, by contrast, has demonstrated it can surge forces when tested, providing genuine deterrence. After the 2023 Banjska incident, NATO increased its peacekeeping presence in Kosovo. Serbia drew down its border deployment, ending the crisis.

The Pentagon is right to ask what the value of an American military presence is worth. For KFOR, the answer is plain: a few hundred U.S. troops are successfully maintaining a quarter-century-long peace that Russia would love to see unravel. Lawmakers from both parties already understand that. The Pentagon should, too, and keep KFOR intact.

Mark Montgomery, a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral, serves as a senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ (FDD), where Ivana Stradner is a research fellow.

Scientists have discovered a bizarre “invisible” object in space that challenges our understanding of stellar evolution and could help resolve longstanding astronomical mysteries, according to a study published on Wednesday in Science Advances . Its orbit and mass are so strange, in fact, that researchers ran thousands of simulations and couldn’t reproduce them.
The hidden object is likely an ultra-rare supermassive neutron star, which is the collapsed core that is left over after a massive star goes supernova. Located in a system called J0008+0128,, the object was detected through its gravitational effects on its companion, a red giant star.
Massive stars that go supernova either collapse into neutron stars or black holes, both of which belong to a wider family of dead stars known as “stellar remnants.” But for decades, astronomers have puzzled over the so-called “mass gap" between neutron stars and black holes, which is the observed scarcity of remnants between 2.5 and five times as massive as the Sun.
The object lurking in J0008+0128 could be up to 2.8 times as massive as the Sun, which “potentially places the unseen companion within the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes,” according to the new study. The colossal mass, combined with its unusually wide orbit of 1,218 days, challenge our understanding of how these objects form.
“We search for compact objects (mainly neutron stars and black holes) using large spectroscopic surveys,” said Song Wang, an associate researcher at the National Astronomical Observatories, Chinese Academy of Sciences, who co-authored the study, in an email to 404 Media. “We have found more than 10 neutron stars, and J0008+0128 is the most massive one among them.”

Generally speaking, stars that are over 25 times as massive as the Sun will form black holes, while stars that are about 10-to-25 times as massive will become neutron stars. Stars with masses similar to the Sun, meanwhile, are destined to spend their afterlives as white dwarfs, which are much larger and less dense than neutron stars. For instance, neutron stars are mere miles in diameter, whereas white dwarfs are about the size of Earth.
Because they are dense pressure cookers, neutron stars are filled with disassembled components of atoms, especially neutrons—hence the name—but also protons and electrons. Supermassive neutron stars like the one in J0008+0128 can shed light on the poorly understood “equation of state” in these objects, which is the relationship between their immense pressures and densities.
“The equation of state of neutron stars is a long-standing unsolved problem in astrophysics, and neutron star masses can provide crucial observational tests,” said Wang. “This is particularly true for massive neutron stars: how massive a neutron star can become depends on how ‘stiff’ its internal matter is in resisting gravitational collapse.”
“The discovery and measurement of supermassive neutron stars (i.e., those above two solar masses) can place important constraints on the equation of state of matter at extreme densities, helping to identify the theories that truly describe the behavior of matter under such extreme conditions,” he added.
In other words, J0008+0128 could open a window into the churning atomic stew within these exotic objects. But the system is weird for reasons beyond the supermassive object lurking in the dark. Indeed, the team ran thousands of simulations but none of them “reproduced physical and orbital properties similar to J0008+0128,” according to the study.
The wide orbit between the neutron star and the red giant star is particularly difficult to explain. Neutron stars could become supermassive by gravitationally tugging material off of their stellar companions, but this object is too far away from the red giant for this mechanism to make sense.
“In fact, many compact objects discovered in recent years cannot be explained by standard binary evolution models and supernova mechanisms,” Wang noted, citing two other examples, known as Gaia BH2 and G3425.

“There may be two massive stars forming an inner binary,” Wang explained. “They can merge at different stages. For example, a neutron star merges with a normal star, or two neutron stars merge. Either case could produce the supermassive neutron star that we observe today.”
“In addition, if J0008+0128 formed through single-star evolution, its discovery would suggest that supernovae can produce massive neutron stars,” he added.

Wang and his colleagues were able to make this new discovery with the help of sophisticated sky surveys, including astrometric data from Europe’s Gaia space telescope. The team hopes that the forthcoming data release from Gaia, due out next month, will help to narrow down the possible mass of the unseen object in J0008+0128.

Key Points

- The Jensen Huang affair is turning Capitol Hill into a pressure cooker, with some lawmakers calling for the country's most important tech CEO to resign amid the scandal.

- The situation may give Congress reason to advance a suite of bills in this year's National Defense Authorization Act to tighten export controls on advanced AI chips.

- What Nvidia does now — and whether Huang remains atop the company — could impact its relationship with Washington and whether lawmakers crack down.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks to media before a roundtable with South Korean AI and robotics startups at the Shilla Hotels, June 8, 2026 in Seoul, South Korea.
Chung Sung-jun | Getty Images

Members of Congress are calling on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign, and momentum is building to subpoena the executive, whose company is a leader in advanced artificial intelligence chips.
Senate banking committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., doubled down Wednesday on his call for Huang to resign, and a key Democratic House oversight panel member and House Republican piled on.

"As a matter of his own conscience, he should resign," Cramer told CNBC, in response to revelations that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy as the chipmaker he co-founded was given permission from the U.S. government to sell its technology to China.
Huang, who leads a company that's been a chief beneficiary of the artificial intelligence boom, on Sunday admitted to having an affair with a woman whom news outlets have reported U.S. intelligence concluded was a Chinese spy . The revelation is sending shockwaves through Washington, with lawmakers now fearing that U.S. AI dominance could be at risk.

# Read more CNBC news on Nvidia

- Is Nvidia too big to fail? Its AI financing web raises the stakes : Analysis

- Nvidia prepares to oust Jensen Huang, WSJ reports — stock sinks further

- Jensen Huang affair rocks D.C., brings calls from Congress to resign

- Inside Nvidia: Jensen Huang's first day in office after affair reveal

- Nvidia hires law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead Jensen Huang affair probe

- Huang affair with alleged Chinese spy complicates Nvidia China problem

- China panel chair Moolenaar demands answers on Nvidia CEO's alleged affair with a Chinese spy

- What is Megaspeed? The Nvidia chip buyer in the spotlight after Jensen Huang's affair

- Read Huang's email to his staff and statement from Nvidia's board of directors

- Nvidia's CEO turmoil gives newly empowered Democrats fresh ammunition in pursuit of oversight

"What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer said, referring to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk."
Cramer's comments come on the deadline set by a trio of House lawmakers who requested Huang to testify before their committees on Nov. 18.

# Subpoena power
GOP Reps. Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee; John Moolenaar, chair of the Permanent Select Committee on China; and Rick Crawford, who leads the House intelligence panel, called for Huang to appear in a Nov. 4 letter . Congress members in the majority party also have subpoena power, should they choose to use it.

Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Wednesday afternoon that they had not yet heard from Huang and that they were giving him until the end of the day to respond.
Asked whether the committees were considering subpoenaing Huang if he doesn't agree to appear, Mast said "yes."
Moolenaar, when asked the same question, said "all three committees have subpoena power, and I know all three committees have a very serious interest in getting to the bottom of this and having transparency around this."
"We are going to continue to pursue this," Moolenaar said.
The lawmakers are far from alone in their criticism, concern and outright shock over the affair. And the scrutiny is only expected to intensify with Democrats poised to take over both chambers of Congress in January. Huang has been close with President Donald Trump during the president's second term, traveling on Air Force One to China in May.
"Jensen Huang should resign from Nvidia," Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., a member of the House Oversight Committee, told CNBC. Subramanyam is the top Democrat on the panel's Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs.
"I didn't agree with his sentiment that there's no downside to exporting chips to China," he said. "But I never thought that he might be having an affair with a Chinese spy who was helping smuggle chips into China at an alarming rate."

Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., gives a thumbs up as he arrives for a House Republican Conference meeting at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, Sept. 10, 2024.
Kent Nishimura | Getty Images

Rep. Don Bacon , R-Neb., who is retiring from Congress after sometimes bucking Trump, also said the CEO should step down.
"From the little I know, yes." Bacon told CNBC in response to whether Huang should resign. "I mean, he allowed himself to get compromised by the Chinese government. Not good."

# Export controls
Huang was notably opposed to strict export controls on AI chips to China, which ruffled feathers with China hawks on Capitol Hill.
Democrats are widely expected to launch myriad investigations into the White House and industry when they assume control of both chambers of Congress in January. Nvidia is now likely to be at the center of those probes.
"There's two parts to this investigation that [need] to happen somewhere immediately," Subramanyam said. "One is what was going on with Nvidia and China, and two is why the administration did nothing about it even though they appeared to have known, and what the administration knew, and what influence the money from Nvidia and Jensen Huang had on this administration, essentially staying silent."
Rep. Jay Obernolte , R-Calif., co-chair of the House AI task force, said Tuesday he hopes that the Huang scandal can avoid becoming a distraction in talks about imposing export controls on advanced AI chips.
The situation may give Congress additional ammunition as it tries to pass a suite of bills in this year's National Defense Authorization Act to tighten export controls on advanced AI chips.
Congress has still not passed the annual defense bill, which is a top priority for lawmakers in the lame-duck session.
Those bills include the AI Overwatch Act , the MATCH Act and the Chip Security Act — all of which are aimed at preventing U.S. chip technology from falling into adversarial hands.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., in a statement following the revelation of Huang's affair, urged their colleagues to include the AI Overwatch Act. Warren, the incoming Senate banking committee chair, sponsored the bill in the Senate with Banks.
"Huang's confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China's intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related," the senators said. "It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips."

**OpenAI's Q3 2026 revenue (reported, not confirmed)**

- **Revenue:** Quarterly revenue reportedly passed $10 billion for the first time. The company attributed this to "strong demand for its recent AI models."
- **Growth:** That is roughly a 50% increase over Q2 revenue of $6.7 billion. Revenue grew about 18% from Q1 ($5.7 billion) to Q2.
- **Profitability:** The adjusted operating margin reportedly improved from -150% in Q2 to -109% in Q3. The article gives no dollar figure for losses.
- **Annual run rate:** Bloomberg reports an annualized revenue run rate of $50 billion.

**Source:** The figures come from a Bloomberg report citing anonymous sources, published November 10, 2026. TechCrunch's Ram Iyer wrote the article on November 11, 2026, and framed the numbers as unverified ("if true").

**Comparison with Anthropic**

- Anthropic reported Q3 revenue of $17 billion, above OpenAI's reported $10 billion.
- Anthropic said its annual revenue run rate rose by $10 billion within a month, to $81 billion as of the end of October. OpenAI's reported run rate is $50 billion.
- The two companies calculate annualized revenue differently. Anthropic counts sales made through its cloud partners, while OpenAI reports only its share of some partner sales.
- Anthropic is leading in enterprise AI and in revenue growth. It is also seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation in an IPO that is expected soon.

**Context**

- OpenAI reportedly improved results through tighter pricing, discounts, better models, and a greater focus on enterprise products and AI agents.
- OpenAI says it has over a billion users, but the article assumes most are free users or subscribers to cheaper plans.
- OpenAI also faces competition from Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and lower-cost open-source models, especially from China.

Gemini Decisions API

Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question.

It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million.

Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.

I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file:

dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it?
robot: Does this video have a robot in it?
france: Is this video set in France?
usa: Is this video set in the USA?

Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that:

}

aws-emulator

Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so.

It's written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents - 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project. Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian wrote about how it came to be in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog.

It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms.

Release: llm 0.37.2

Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w.

LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers.

Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1.

response.result:
**Publication date and time:** The page shows only an update stamp: November 12, 2026, 5:22 AM EST. No original publication time appears.

**What the board is reportedly preparing to do:** According to the article, Nvidia's board "is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang soon." The article attributes this to the board's reported plans, which were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

**Sourcing:** The report cites "two sources familiar with the matter." The article also says the Trump administration is aware of the matter, per those sources.

**Share price move:** Nvidia's share price "slid more than 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday." The article gives no closing price.

**Nvidia board statement:** On Sunday, the board said it had launched an independent investigation into allegations that the CEO "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." It also said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

**Second affair:** The article does not describe a second affair. It covers one alleged extramarital affair, with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly believe was a Chinese asset. The article names Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, as the woman with whom the NYT reported he had a close relationship. She previously led Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based firm that bought billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips and hardware. Jensen Huang's message to employees did not name the woman involved.

AUTH: Chenhui Hu, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
SUBJ: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

ABS: Understanding the internal representations of neural networks and characterizing their relationship with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. - **The main tool is litigation.** The order directed the Attorney General to set up an AI Litigation Task Force, which the DOJ created on January 9, 2026. Colorado's AI Act was named in the executive order's text as an example and became the first case the task force intervened in.
- **Some areas are carved out.** The order specifies certain carve-outs: (i) child safety protections; (ii) AI computing and data center infrastructure; (iii) state government procurement and use of AI.
- **Compliance advice is unchanged.** Several law firms advise clients to continue complying with applicable state AI laws, since an executive order cannot itself overturn state statutes.

Sources also differ on the order's details. One source refers to a June 2, 2026 order alongside the December 2025 one, which I could not verify. If you need something tied to November 11, 2026 specifically, such as a new order, a court ruling, or a congressional action, the search would need a different query.

**Publication:** November 11, 2026, 2:37 PM EST (MoneyWatch, by Megan Cerullo)

**What United said and changed:** United said on Wednesday that it is banning AI agents from making flight reservations for travelers. It cited security risks and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules. The airline is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.

**Exact policy wording:**
- "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information"
- "actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."
- "United is taking steps to restrict access" to "prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants"

The airline says it will restrict access directly on its digital platforms and indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators.

**Federal rules:** United said that using an AI agent to check in for a flight could violate federal rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage contains no banned substances.

**Effective dates:** The article gives no effective date. It says only that the announcement came on Wednesday.

**Named AI agents and companies:**
- Meta's Muse
- OpenAI's dots
- ChatGPT (Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to its users)
- Southwest Airlines, which is taking a different approach
- Kayak, Hopper, and Google Flights, where United fares will remain bookable
- Google, Atmosphere Research Group (analyst Henry Harteveldt's firm)

**Spokesperson:** The article does not name a United spokesperson. The policy statement is attributed only to "the airline." Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group, commented separately. He said the policy suggests United wants to keep control of the booking process and avoid the cost of AI bot flight searches.

**Numbers:** The article includes no dollar amounts, percentages, or other statistics.

input.prompt: Publication date. What exactly is being announced? Quote all benchmark numbers, pricing, model names, availability, and any limitations Google states. Quote numbers exactly as written.

response.result:
**Publication date:** Nov 11, 2026

**What's announced:** Google is launching the Gemini Decisions API, "a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions," powered by the Gemini Decision 1 model (`gemini-decision-1`). It supports yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scoring over text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. Each answer includes a confidence score from 0 to 1.

**Benchmarks:**
- The article says Gemini Decision 1 "leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error." It gives no specific scores in the text. The results appear only in charts.
- Latency: "150-250 ms end-to-end latency," with "50-100 ms of model compute."
- Cost: "nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API."
- Gemini Notebook routing: "up to 40% lower latency" for everyday queries.

**Pricing:** "$0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed." The article also offers "an API no-cost tier" in Google AI Studio for prototyping, and says there are no output-token or separate audio transcription and OCR charges.

**Capacity:** Inputs of up to 256K tokens and up to 1,000 questions per request. Choice questions take 2 to 255 options.

**Availability:**
- Available now through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio.
- Support for Gemini in Google Cloud is "coming soon."
- Integrations with OpenRouter, LangChain, Vercel, LiteLLM, and others are "rolling out."

**Limitations:**
- The API is for bounded, closed-set decisions. It scores options rather than generating open-ended text.
- The latency figures are reported for contexts up to 16K tokens.
- The page's AI-generated summary notes that "Generative AI is experimental."

It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. # ARTEX and AI-Powered Red Teaming Tools: What Defenders Need to Know

6 min read

-

By:
- Cuong Dinh

- Richard Emerson

- Samantha Stallings

-

Published: November 11, 2026

- Categories:
- General

- Insights

- Tags:
- GenAI

- LLM

- Penetration testing

-

-

Share

-

-

-

-

-

-

-

A rapidly expanding ecosystem of AI-enabled tools such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI — marketed for red teaming and penetration testing — are being used by attackers to execute offensive operations autonomously.

Their footprint is already substantial. Unit 42 has observed ARTEX used in intrusion attempts against multiple targets .

Our Incident Response team investigated multiple intrusions in which the attacker’s server hosted an ARTEX console or used infrastructure and user agents associated with ARTEX.

Separately, Unit 42 Managed Threat Hunting tracked a coordinated ARTEX campaign against customer cloud environments in sectors worldwide, including retail and consulting.

External scrutiny has already disrupted project lifecycles: the author of ARTEX recently made the repository closed-source and ceased public development to prevent misuse . Emerging alternatives are rapidly filling the void, introducing new capabilities that threat actors will inevitably co-opt.

Here, we share our observations of how attackers are using AI-powered red team tools, along with our recommendations for how defenders can mitigate.

# Why Is ARTEX Such an Effective Tool for Attackers?

ARTEX and other red-teaming platforms are free, quick to deploy and need little more than access to a large language model (LLM).

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent AI penetration testing framework first published in mid-2026. It has been widely forked since.

Attackers can use ARTEX to evaluate responses, adapt when something fails and keep pursuing their objective. They can target the identity workflows and APIs that organizations expose to the internet, and then use the associated credentials and trust relationships to reach the cloud.

# AI-Powered Red Teaming and Pentesting Ecosystem Infrastructure

As of October 2026, Unit 42 identified 1,323 internet-facing hosts running CyberStrikeAI and 609 running ARTEX. Notably, 21 hosts were running both at the same time.

Unit 42 analyzed 14 tools across the pentesting and red-teaming tool ecosystem, highlighting 12 emerging tools alongside CyberStrikeAI and ARTEX.

These tools can be broken down into four categories of AI assisted red team activities.

Category
Tools
Goal

Reconnaissance and attack-surface management
ARL, ARL-Next, Scope Sentry, Nemo, XingRin, OpenEASD
Identify what assets exist, what is exposed and what changes

Agent-led testing and vulnerability hunting
CyberStrikeAI, ARTEX, Cairn, PentAGI, AutoHunter
Manage what should be investigated and how the system can act on it

Source-code auditing and verification
DeepAudit, AIxVuln
Identify where source code might be vulnerable and what supports that finding

AI-system security assessment
AI-Infra-Guard
Identify if AI infrastructure, agents, tools and model interfaces are vulnerable or unreliable

Table 1. Tool categories.

# Implications For Defenders

Defenders should be aware of the following implications of AI-powered red teaming platforms:

# Lowered Skill Floor for Attackers

Adversaries no longer require specialized tradecraft to execute multi-stage, adaptive penetration testing.

Off-the-shelf tooling combined with LLMs like DeepSeek allows financially motivated actors to launch and manage dozens of complex, concurrent network intrusions for minimal compute cost.

# Risk of Internet-Exposed Assets

Any internet-exposed asset, regardless of organizational size or sector, is equally likely to be impacted by automated, persistent intrusion attempts.

Attackers using the autonomous AI penetration testing framework ARTEX are turning public password reset pages and exposed APIs into a path to cloud access, sometimes in less than a day. Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability.

Because these autonomous platforms cannot target what they cannot find, continuous discovery and mitigation of exposed edge assets remains an effective barrier against automated campaigns.

Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams

Alignment Science Blog

# Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams

Sahan Paliskara 1
Nattaput Namchittai 1 , Jacqueline Tay 2 , and Avery Griffin 3
Andrew Lampinen 3
November 11, 2026

1 Anthropic Fellows Program; 2 Independent; 3 Anthropic

tl;dr
As AI agents become more capable and widely used, they are increasingly required to interact with each other. Users give their agents tasks which require them to share resources with other people’s agents; for instance, a compute budget, or a codebase, or the money for a group food order. These settings are understudied, so we built four environments with simulated users and everyday tasks and tested frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Alibaba in them. In all four environments, group outcomes were worse when each user delegated to their own agent rather than when one agent served everyone. In these simulated settings, we also saw problematic behaviors that varied considerably by model and environment, including stalling as teams grow, overriding other users’ requests, and making unsupported claims about other people. Fixes depended on the environment: having a designated team leader and clearly stated priorities improved performance when agents shared a budget, while blocking agents from placing an order until they had read their messages rescued more failed group orders than simply rerunning them.

We are releasing three of the environments as a benchmark, MAMUBench, so that others can use them to test how well agents coordinate, and how they behave, in multi-user, multi-agent systems.

📄 Paper · 💻 Code

Research done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program .

# Introduction

As AI agents become more common, users increasingly deploy them to pursue goals that require interacting with other agents. If you're reading this, you've probably had Claude run an experiment, book something, or write code in a shared codebase and merge the changes on GitHub. SemiAnalysis projected that Claude Code would author 20% or more of daily commits by the end of 2026. Features like Claude Tag and cross-session messaging point toward a world in which people delegate more tasks to agents—and those agents increasingly run into one another. Recent releases also let several users share resources through their agents: with the DoorDash CLI , several people's agents can add to one group cart; Slack Code brings agents such as Claude, Devin and GitHub Copilot into channels the whole team works in; and OpenAI's dots give each person an agent that works on their behalf, in a space shared with teammates (DevDay 2026 recap ). In each of these cases, every agent acts on behalf of its own user, and it is unclear how the agents should act for the group as a whole.

Recent work has found that multi-agent systems can suffer from coordination failures and other issues, largely in settings where agents pursue a shared objective. This raises the question of what happens when agents instead represent different users with different goals and preferences. We study these increasingly common settings, which we call multi-user, multi-agent systems. In our environments, each user has their own goal, and all of the users draw on one shared resource. We evaluate a range of frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Alibaba on these environments. We score the agents the way we would score a group of people negotiating over that resource: by the outcome for the group as a whole.

# Setup

We developed four environments for this multi-user, multi-agent setting: an API-token budget shared by researchers, a clinic calendar shared by urgent patients, a group food order or travel booking that users arrange through personal assistants, and a merge queue with a release cutoff. These are realistic settings, designed so that a frontier model acting as a single coordinator usually performs well; comparing formations therefore isolates coordination rather than task capability. We compare four formations: solo (one user, one agent); a coordinator , a single agent that serves several users; a silent team, one agent per user with no way to communicate; and a peer-to-peer team , one agent per user with a channel between the agents. We use the coordinator as our control. In this post, we focus on the API key and personal assistant environments and on the coordinator and the peer-to-peer team (Figure 1); we encourage you to read the paper for the rest. Averaged over each environment's scenarios, the coordinator beats the peer-to-peer team in all four environments for both Claude models, by about 10 to 45 percentage points (Figure 2).

The formations we use to organize the agents (the paper has two more) and some interesting behaviors in our environments, described below.

One agent for everyone beats a team of per-user agents in all four environments, for both Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5. Bars show the group's outcome as a share of what the best possible strategy achieves, averaged over scenarios. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals.

In June, AMD overtook the predictive memory engine known as MEXT, which claims to offer upwards of 99% of the performance of a system with full DRAM capacity while running with as little as 25% of the physical DIMMs. The technology offloads cold memory pages to flash storage and uses an AI model to serve pages before they’re needed, and AMD says it plans to extend the tech across a wide swath of its IT infrastructure next year.

The pitch behind MEXT seems too good to be true. According to AMD and MEXT founder Gary Smerdon, the technology can cut the physical DRAM required in a server by 20% to 75% depending on the application and performance target. That missing memory still registers as installed DRAM to the OS. Instead of DRAM, however, MEXT uses relatively inexpensive flash storage to offload cold pages, flying them back in as they’re needed with an AI model. In some of AMD’s internal workloads, such as Synopsys PrimeTime, the company says it’s able to achieve 95% of the performance of a full server while running at 50% DRAM capacity with MEXT.
AMD has deployed MEXT internally on 145 servers, which it says will expand to 2,000 servers next year. In addition, the company has announced a partnership with HPE to bring MEXT to customers. Currently, we’re in phase 1 of the rollout, with some EPYC Venice servers carrying a “MEXT Ready” badge and a dedicated NVMe drive or bay for the offload. Phase 2 brings MEXT licenses out to these servers, as well as the RAM View application. AMD hasn’t said when Phase 2 will begin.
Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware

Watch full video here:

The AI-driven DRAM pricing surge impacts more than just gaming PCs, with enterprises also feeling the brunt of price increases, even if they aren’t running AI workloads. If MEXT is able to achieve what AMD claims, it could be transformative given the current market. Because of that, it’s worth understanding what exactly MEXT is, as well as what AMD claims it can do.

Although MEXT is exciting in concept, it’s obvious that AMD is taking a conservative approach to the rollout. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, after all. The applications of MEXT are currently narrow, though AMD says it’s expanding the workloads it’s using MEXT on with promising early results.

# DRAM, Flash and an LLM

(Image credit: AMD)
The basic setup of MEXT is simple in concept: cold pages go to flash, AI brings those pages back as needed, and it’s as if the memory was never missing in the first place. The main problem should be obvious. Flash is orders of magnitude slower than DRAM, so streaming pages back into memory from flash as they’re needed isn’t feasible. MEXT’s trick is using an AI model to predict the pages you’ll need. And, as long as the model is able to stay ahead by at least the transfer latency from the SSD, it’s as if the physical DRAM was installed the whole time.
This isn’t a crazy concept considering how a transformer-based LLM, which MEXT uses, operates. If you’re unfamiliar with the inner workings, this open-source visualization breaks down the concept of a transformer AI model cleanly. response.stdout:
We tested whether targeted changes, such as added instructions or a lead agent with decision authority, close these gaps (Figure 5). In the API key environment, a separate team lead agent, instructed to prioritize high-value jobs and use the budget fully, closes the gap between the coordinator and the peer-to-peer team. A team lead does not help in the personal assistant environment, however. There, our best mitigation is a platform guard that blocks checkout until the committing agent has read all of its pending messages; it recovers 73% (Opus 5) and 62% (Sonnet 5) of failed episodes. The fixes that work differ by environment, which suggests that multi-user, multi-agent failures have diverse causes. We cover mitigations in more depth in the paper.

Mitigation results for Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5. API key (left): a team lead brings the peer-to-peer team up to the coordinator or above, and three added instructions improve it further: (1) the lead ranks jobs strictly by value, (2) it releases any budget it holds back while there's still time to use it, and (3) every other agent reports its jobs' information and follows the lead's allocation. Personal assistant (right): the bottom two rows rerun failed team episodes. Here, an unread-message guard recovers most of them. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals.

# Discussion and Implications for Safety

Multi-user, multi-agent systems are already emerging. For example, Instinct recently released its Trusted Person Network , in which each user's assistant can talk to other users' assistants to coordinate plans on their behalf. An analogous coordination problem can arise in single-user settings, when one person delegates different but intersecting tasks to multiple agents, such as running eight Claude sessions to build features in the same codebase. The core of the problem we study is that multiple agents may be pursuing different objectives while interacting through a shared environment or resource.

Our results, together with prior work, show that multi-user, multi-agent systems carry risks beyond worse group outcomes: an agent acting for one user can harm others who share the system. In our environments, agents from a range of providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, and Alibaba) acted on other users' jobs without consent, overrode a user's request, and made claims about other people that their information did not support. Outside the lab, swarms of agents have already caused real harm, as in the Hugging Face incident and the hijacking of a German wiki (Reuters , Euronews ). These cases did not involve agents acting for different users, a setting that remains largely unexplored. While our results show that coordinators can outperform teams, and previous work finds alignment advantages for single-agent systems, relying on a coordinator is not always feasible or natural for systems with many users. Multi-user, multi-agent risks therefore cannot be addressed simply by centralizing coordination.

These results suggest concrete next steps. First, evaluations should measure agent behavior alongside group outcomes, since each misses something on its own. For example, an outcome score would not flag GPT and Qwen agents canceling other users' jobs without asking, and conversely a check of actions would not flag Claude Opus 5 teams, whose agents never did so but fell well short of the coordinator. Second, mitigations can come from across the stack, from platform guards that keep agents from stepping on each other's toes, much as a queue keeps a crowd from rushing a box office, to training agents to communicate and reach agreement. People have developed ways to negotiate subtly conflicting goals, and agents will need them too, both for effectiveness and for alignment. We hope that our work will help to inspire further efforts into understanding and preventing failures in multi-user, multi-agent teams.

The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/11/11/global-socket-how-threat-actors-weaponizing-gsocket-stealthy-c2/

Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:49:57 +0000

https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/?p=150921

Threat actors are deploying GSocket on compromised Linux servers to keep encrypted remote access after the original vulnerability is patched. Learn how to detect, investigate, and remediate this activity.

The post The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2 appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

]]>
Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block.

# When one RCE stops being just one RCE

Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it.

To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions.

GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it.

- Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself.

- Outbound-only connections. The compromised host and the operator both connect outbound to the relay, which bridges the two sessions. The host needs no inbound listener or public IP address, and network address translation does not prevent the connection. Inbound firewall rules do not see this traffic, although egress filtering and outbound monitoring can.

- Built-in evasion and persistence. The deployment script can rename the process, stage files in memory-backed directories, and install persistence that survives a reboot, without additional development by the threat actor.

The same relay model that supports legitimate remote administration also gives threat actors a way to maintain access without operating dedicated C2 infrastructure. Once GSocket runs on a compromised server, the server and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network, which pairs the two sessions over an end-to-end encrypted channel.

Figure 1: After code execution on an internet-facing application, GSocket is deployed and both ends connect outward to the relay.

Because GSocket runs independently of the exploited application, patching the vulnerability does not remove the relay client or its persistence.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows that this activity is not limited to a single compromise. From March through August 2026, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2%, although the increase was not consistent month to month.

Figure 2: Growth in GSocket-related detections from March to August, measured against the March baseline.

Web applications and hosting accounted for 87.1% of attributable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint incidents in the analysed telemetry. Within that group, PHP web applications and cPanel hosting represented 63.9% of incidents and Apache represented 24.3% (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Distribution of GSocket-related incidents by application category. PHP web applications and Apache account for most incidents within the web applications and hosting group.

Education and research accounted for the largest share of affected organizations (30.7%), followed by technology and telecommunications (22.9%).

Reports from November 11–12, 2026 say Nvidia's board was weighing whether to remove CEO Jensen Huang, but none of the results report a final decision.

- **Stock drop:** Shares fell more than 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the reports, closing up 2.9% at $173.73 in regular trading before the drop. Premarket on Thursday they were down 7.2% shortly after 10:00 CET.
- **Board meeting:** The board met late Wednesday US time to decide whether to remove Huang, Reuters reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. - **Market impact:** The drop continued a steep decline in the company's market value, which has sunk more than $450 billion since Nvidia announced the probe.

The results don't confirm whether Huang has been removed or whether the board has reached a decision. Any update after the Thursday reports would need a new search.

**Greece's AI Act framework: key facts**

- **Law:** Law 5321/2026, which sets Greece's national governance, innovation, and enforcement framework for the EU AI Act.
- **Adopted:** Summer 2026. The Ministry of Digital Governance opened public consultation on 21 June, and the consultation closed on 6 July. The law was finalized and enacted within two weeks of that closing.
- **Publication and effect:** Published 20 July 2026. It takes effect on that date unless a specific provision says otherwise.
- **Oversight model:** Oversight is spread across existing sectoral regulators. Greece did not create a standalone AI authority.
- **Designated authority:** The Hellenic Data Protection Authority (HDPA) is the market surveillance authority for prohibited AI practices, Annex III high-risk systems, and Article 50 transparency obligations. It is also Greece's single point of contact with the Commission and other member states.
- **Related EU timeline:** The Commission and national authorities began enforcing the AI Act on 2 August 2026, when new transparency rules took effect. The Commission's AI Office centrally supervises general-purpose AI models.
