- **Announcement:** The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) announced its 2027 coordinated enforcement action, focused on automated decision-making technology (ADMT) in employment.
- **Publication date:** 11 November 2026.
- **Framework:** It is the sixth action under the EDPB's Coordinated Enforcement Framework (CEF).
- **Scope:** EDPB members and the European Data Protection Supervisor will voluntarily conduct compliance reviews of GDPR provisions on:
  - The right not to be subject to decisions "based solely on automated processing" (Article 22).
  - The right of access, as it applies to ADMT-driven candidate screening tools.
- **Number of DPAs:** The article does not state how many data protection authorities will participate.
- **Timeline:** The action takes place in 2027. The article gives no specific start or reporting dates for it. The final report on the separate 2026 transparency action is not expected until early 2027.
- **Context:** The EDPB has not issued ADMT-specific work since the Article 29 Working Party's May 2018 guidance on Article 22.

{"stdout":"# API Key In the API key environment, groups of four, eight, or 16 researchers share a limited API-token budget. Notably, this budget is not enough to cover everybody's work. Each researcher gives their agent a queue of jobs, along with context on each job's deadline and the consequences of missing it, such as an upcoming paper deadline or a launch review after the weekend. Agents need to cancel and scale down jobs to make sure that some work gets finished. We built 25 scenarios that vary the users and their jobs. We find that peer-to-peer teams reach 47% and 38% of the coordinator's performance for Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5, respectively (30% and 12% of the optimal outcome, against 64% and 32% for the coordinator). The multi-agent team's main problem is that agents act too little and too late. This environment is dynamic, so agents need to sequence jobs actively. Simply allowing, say, a hero run to continue when it has little chance of finishing can consume the remaining time and cause jobs to miss the deadline. In fact, many agents never act at all, and more of them sit out as the team grows: from four to 16 agents, the share that ever act falls from 66% to 10% for Sonnet 5 and from 82% to 25% for GPT-5.6-sol. GPT and Qwen agents also cancel or stop other users' jobs without asking, 3.9 to 7.1 times per episode, against 0.59 for Sonnet 5 and never for Opus 5. These unconsented cuts do not lower the group's outcome, since canceling low-value jobs is what the environment requires, but they are still undesirable because they end another user's work without that user's agreement. Episodes in which agents canceled or shrank other users' jobs without asking usually got a higher group score than episodes in the same scenario where they didn't. But that reveals the limitations of the scoring system: it only looks at the total value of the jobs completed, not whether anyone had their work destroyed or whether they agreed to it. Lastly, the agents' implicit priorities differ from model to model. For example, Claude Opus 5 spreads outcomes across users more evenly than Claude Sonnet 5 and the GPT models (Figure 3). API key behaviors of five models, one row each: Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-5.6-terra, and Qwen3.8-max. As teams grow, fewer agents take any action (left). GPT and Qwen agents also often cancel or stop other users' jobs without asking (middle: unconsented cuts per episode; consent judged by Claude Sonnet 5). Opus 5 spreads outcomes across users more evenly than Sonnet 5 and the GPT models (right: Jain index over the four-user scenarios). Error bars are 95% intervals. # Personal Assistant In the personal assistant environment, groups of users delegate a shared planning task to their own assistants: a group food order, a prepaid reservation, or a travel booking, with a shared budget. In each scenario, one user makes a targeted request, which we call the ask: either a safety constraint or an altruistic request. Importantly, these requests require agents to deviate from default behavior in a reasonable way. For example, a user with celiac disease asks for two plain gluten-free sides instead of an entree. We measure success by whether the final order or booking honors the ask. Across the 25 scenarios, the coordinator honors the ask about twice as often as the peer-to-peer team. Although the ask usually gets communicated within the group, the main problem is a race condition: the agent that commits the order often does so before it has read every message sent to it. Across all scenarios and models, the ask was sent to the agent that placed the final order or booking in 94–99% of episodes, but it was in that agent's context at the time of the commit in only 47–67% (Figure 4). Interestingly, even when the ask was in context, only 56–68% of episodes honored it, against 19–36% when it was not. Teams also tend to override each other's requests in the shared cart or booking: 65–77% of team episodes included at least one edit against the ask. We include results for GPT-5.6-sol and GPT-5.6-terra in the paper as well. Lastly, agents sometimes made claims about other people that their information did not support. Just over half of Claude team episodes contained at least one of these fabrications (58% for Opus 5 and 53% for Sonnet 5, as judged by Claude Opus 5), while a single agent does this in 17–20% of episodes. This follows from how information is split. Each agent sees only its own user's notes but has to talk about everyone's order, so agents fill the gaps: they assume the table wants what their own user wants, attach one user's notes to another, or say a user agreed to something they never said. Behaviors of Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5 teams over all 25 personal assistant scenarios. The ask almost always reaches the agent that places the order, but agents are too eager and often check out before it is in their context (top two rows). When it isn't, the ask is honored far less often (bottom two rows). Agents also fabricate claims about other agents and their users that their information doesn't support (right; judged by Claude Opus 5). Error bars are 95% confidence intervals. # Mitigations We tested whether targeted changes, such as added instructions or a lead agent with decision authority, close these gaps (Figure 5). In the API key environment, a separate team lead agent, instructed to prioritize high-value jobs and use the budget fully, closes the gap between the coordinator and the peer-to-peer team. A team lead does not help in the personal assistant environment, however. There, our best mitigation is a platform guard that blocks checkout until the committing agent has read all of its pending messages; it recovers 73% (Opus 5) and 62% (Sonnet 5) of failed episodes. The fixes that work differ by environment, which suggests that multi-user, multi-agent failures have diverse causes. By John Power

Published On 12 Nov 2026 12 Nov 2026

Chip giant Nvidia’s stock price has tumbled amid reports that its board of directors is meeting to consider the future of CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia shares fell 8.6 percent in after-hours trading on Wednesday as questions swirled over Huang’s position at the top of the $4.2 trillion company.

# Recommended Stories

- list 4 of 4 Nvidia shares plunge amid reports board to discuss CEO Huang’s future

The plunge comes after The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times reported that Nvidia’s board of directors would discuss Huang’s position over allegations that he engaged in an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia employee, in addition to an affair with a woman accused of working with Chinese intelligence services.
Nvidia, which launched an investigation into Huang on Sunday, did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, is one of the most visible faces of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, spearheading the development of high-end graphics processing units used to train and run frontier models.
The leather jacket-sporting tech executive’s position has also placed him at the centre of the geopolitical rivalry between the United States and China, which are locked in a battle for supremacy in AI.
As a confidant of US President Donald Trump, Huang has lobbied for the easing of restrictions on exports of high-end chips to China, putting him at odds with national security hawks in Washington who argue that Beijing must be blocked from access to cutting-edge US tech.

# Seismic moment
If Nvidia’s board were to oust Huang, 63, it would mark a seismic moment for the chip giant.
Advertisement

Viewed as integral to Nvidia’s meteoric rise to the ranks of the world’s most valuable companies, Huang is known for a centralised leadership style that places him at the centre of the company’s day-to-day operations and strategic decisions.
“Jensen is Nvidia; without him, the company loses its central, animating spirit,” Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners in San Francisco, told Al Jazeera.
“The organisation is built around him and replacing him will be very painful organisationally, and impossible to do personality-wise.”
It is unclear whether Nvidia has a succession plan, and analysts see few obvious candidates to take Huang’s place.
Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said Huang has been the “hearts and lungs” of Nvidia and that investors will closely scrutinise the executive’s possible replacement.
“We believe Nvidia’s value is $300 per share with Jensen as CEO and $225 per share without Jensen as CEO,” Ives said in a note to clients, adding that the company would navigate the turmoil and “remain a core foundational piece of the AI Revolution.”
“Jensen is not replaceable by another CEO or group of interim executives, but Nvidia likely now has to move on without Jensen at the helm, which seemed like a Twilight Zone episode narrative before Sunday afternoon when the news broke,” Ives said.

# International intrigue
Nvidia has been the focus of international intrigue over the past week amid reports that Huang had a relationship with a Chinese woman who US intelligence officials determined had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security.
US officials have not provided evidence for the claims about the woman, a Chinese tech executive named Alice Huang.
Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, has not publicly commented on the allegations.

Introduction

Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM).

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Google requires OEMs go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot. As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future. A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors. This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices.

We worked closely with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to analyze this malware ecosystem and disrupt its operations.

While we expect this disruption to have a significant effect on these criminal operations, this is not the end of our work combatting malicious activity. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain. Point-in-time disruptions are a critical tool to protect our users, but lasting disruption in this fluid ecosystem will require continued targeting of this infrastructure.

Google undertook the following actions to support disruption of the XCPE botnet:

  • Legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install malware modules

  • Legal action to take down C2 domains used by over a dozen malware families loaded as modules via this backdoor

  • Banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building and selling certified Android devices in the future, or supplying software to other certified vendors

  • Implementing improvements to how we ensure the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices

Overview

The x.cpe network was built for ongoing profit. By giving malware affiliates backdoor access, the operators conspired to monetize these devices long after purchase.

results:
The search didn't return the Tom's Hardware article itself, so these findings come from AMD's own case study and secondary coverage.

- **Deployment plan:** AMD IT's internal plan anticipates approximately 700 servers by March 2027, with projected cumulative savings of around $21 million. With a full deployment of 2,000 servers expected by the end of 2027, AMD IT projects savings exceeding $60 million.
- **Results so far:** The pilot added about 58TB of capacity, and AMD estimates that buying the same amount as DRAM would have cost about $3.3 million. An earlier version of the case study reported 20% more usable memory at 82% lower expansion cost than equivalent DRAM; estimated savings of $2.78 million across ~90 servers.
- **Technology:** MEXT's software moves cold data from DRAM into NAND flash, then predicts which pages an application will need next and pulls those pages back into DRAM before the request. AMD announced on June 15 that it had acquired MEXT.
- **Market context:** AMD's case study cites TrendForce's forecast of another 10–15% quarterly increase in conventional DRAM contract prices for the fourth quarter, and TrendForce expects DRAM prices to continue to rise and server supply to remain constrained.
- **Caveat:** Flash is slower than DRAM. One analysis notes that flash carries higher write amplification and wear than DRAM; sustained page-swap workloads at scale could erode the claimed 50% cost savings over equipment lifetimes. The 2,000-server and $60 million figures are AMD's own internal projections, not independently verified.

Introduction

\n

Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM).

\n

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

\n

We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

\n

Google requires OEMs go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot. As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future. A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors. This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices.

\n

We worked closely with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to analyze this malware ecosystem and disrupt its operations.

\n

While we expect this disruption to have a significant effect on these criminal operations, this is not the end of our work combatting malicious activity. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain. Point-in-time disruptions are a critical tool to protect our users, but lasting disruption in this fluid ecosystem will require continued targeting of this infrastructure.

\n

Google undertook the following actions to support disruption of the XCPE botnet:

\n
    \n
  • \n

    Legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install malware modules

    \n
    • \n
  • \n

    Legal action to take down C2 domains used by over a dozen malware families loaded as modules via this backdoor

    \n
    • \n
  • \n

    Banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building and selling certified Android devices in the future, or supplying software to other certified vendors

    \n
    • \n
  • \n

    Implementing improvements to how we ensure the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices

    \n
    • \n
\n

Overview

\n

The x.cpe network was built for ongoing profit. By giving malware affiliates backdoor access, the operators conspired to monetize these devices long after purchase.

\n
\n\n
\n

results:
I found no confirmation in these results that the proposal was actually published. The most recent reports are previews, and they point to November 11, 2026.

- **Timing:** A Euronews report dated November 9, 2026 says the EU will announce its proposal for the Digital Fairness Act on Wednesday. CMS Law gives a similar date, saying a draft of the long-awaited Digital Fairness Act is expected on 11 November 2026.
- **Dark patterns:** According to a draft Euronews says it saw, the European Commission plans to ban ten manipulative website and app designs outright. Examples in the reporting include fake scarcity notices and pre-ticked add-ons.
- **AI:** The results mention AI mainly as a scope question. One list of expected priorities includes unfair use of AI systems for commercial purposes. The Commission also is still considering how the DFA would interact with existing frameworks, such as the UCPD or AI Act. These sources are from before the release, so they don't show what the final text says on AI.
- **Open questions:** An earlier Fieldfisher analysis noted that the legal form of the act (regulation or directive) has not been confirmed.

Verify against the Commission's official press release or the proposal text before relying on any of this, since the sources are pre-publication reports and one is a leak.

results:
The Commission's Digital Fairness Act proposal was published on 11 November 2026, and the results agree on its main points, though some details differ between sources.

- **Date and scope:** One source says the proposed regulation seeks to address practices including dark patterns, addictive design, unfair personalisation, problematic influencer marketing and spending-maximising features in digital products.
- **Addictive design:** Article 17 requires traders to offer tools for switching off addictive features. Those features include autoplay, endless feeds, and engagement nudges tied to penalties or lost benefits (Article 17 specifically addresses addictive design. Traders would have to provide consumers with accessible and effective tools to disable the addictive features). A critic from EDRi argues that offering an opt-out should not count as enough ("Offering an opt-out should not automatically be considered sufficient," she said.).
- **Personalised pricing:** Article 13 would limit profiling-based personalised pricing where it is reasonably likely to harm minors or vulnerable consumers (Article 13 would restrict personalised pricing based on profiling where it is reasonably likely to cause harm to minors or vulnerable consumers.). Another source says the text does not ban dynamic pricing as such; it demands transparency.
- **Manipulative design:** Article 10 would bar interface designs likely to materially distort consumers' economic decisions (traders would be prohibited from designing or organising online interfaces in ways likely to materially distort consumers' economic behaviour.).
- **Enforcement and penalties:** One report puts the maximum fine at 6% of annual global turnover, the same ceiling as the Digital Services Act (DSA). Another says the addictive design rules would be enforced by Digital Services Coordinators against online platform providers (The addictive design rules would be enforced by the Digital Services Coordinators against providers of online platforms).
- **Next steps:** The proposal now goes to the European Parliament and the Council.

Two caveats: one commentary (EUobserver) discusses a leaked draft, so its wording may differ from the final text. Also, the sources conflict on how strong the personalised-pricing limits are, so check the official text before relying on the details.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 11, 2026. The Commission published the proposal that morning, and the article is dated the same day.

**Official proposal:** COM(2026) 1100 final, "Proposal for a Digital Fairness Act." The source links to it at https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/0575d59f-554f-4a9e-b54b-e6b717175809_en?filename=Proposal%20for%20a%20Digital%20Fairness%20Act.pdf

**Key facts**

- **Structure:** The DFA would repeal the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and replace it with a regulation covering B2C commercial practices, both online and offline. Chapter III, "Digital fairness," covers Articles 10–29.
- **Dark patterns:** Article 10 prohibits them. Article 5 treats violations as unfair commercial practices. Annex I lists banned dark patterns.
- **Addictive design:** Article 17 requires tools that let consumers disable features such as autoplay and notifications. It does not prohibit them for adults.
- **Enforcement:** Article 30 gives the Commission direct enforcement powers. Article 34 concerns private enforcement and evidentiary support.
- **Other articles:** Article 3(3) (continued use as a "transactional decision"), Article 5(3) (vulnerability), Article 11 (influencer marketing), Article 15 (loot boxes), Article 20 (free trial conversion), Article 25 (human customer service).

**AI and profiling provisions**

- **Article 12:** Bans targeted ads to minors where the trader is aware with reasonable certainty the consumer is a minor, and bans profiling using special categories of data under GDPR Article 9(1). Recital 59 extends personalized recommendations to "natural language systems."
- **Article 13:** Conditionally bans personalized pricing targeting minors or vulnerable consumers where it is reasonably likely to cause harm. Recital 60 exempts personalization that benefits consumers, such as student rebates.
- **Article 26:** Bans interfaces that force consumers to use automated systems to access or conclude transactions (26(9)). Automated contracting tools must offer parameter controls and disclose payments and conflicts of interest (26(1)–(4)). Article 26 does not apply to financial services.
- **Not fully addressed:** The authors say the proposal's handling of AI agents and price personalization still needs scrutiny.

**Fine levels**

- The proposal, as described in this article, does not set EU-level fine amounts. Member States would define them, which the authors criticize.
- For comparison, the article cites a 10 million EUR fine imposed by Italy in 2018 under the UCPD against Facebook, and a $25 billion New Mexico judgment against Meta. That judgment followed a potential calculation of about $219.5 billion at a $5,000 statutory maximum per violation. Neither is a DFA penalty.

# Anthropic signs another $4.3bn in compute agreements with Microsoft

May cancel contract with neocloud Lambda

November 11, 2026

By

Georgia Butler

Have your say

In a new filing from Anthropic in the lead-up to its initial public offering, the AI lab has revealed some changes to its cloud contracts.
The company has added up to $4.3bn in compute agreements with Microsoft, as first reported by The Information .

– Anthropic

At the start of November, a filing stated that Anthropic had an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, “substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.”
Of that, the hyperscale-committed spend was $121.3bn to lease compute from Google, $120.5bn in capacity from SpaceX, $110bn from Amazon, and $44.9bn from Microsoft.
The Microsoft agreement is now valued at least at $47.2 billion and up to $49.2 billion, adding a potential $4.3bn to Anthropic's cloud spend.
The filing further notes that its $34.9bn contract with Lambda (part of a larger $41.3bn commitment) is now terminable by either party.
"Under our August 2026 agreement, which represents approximately $34.9 billion of the aggregate commitment, either party may terminate if Lambda does not secure the facility lease by a specific date. Lambda did not secure the facility lease by such date and, as a result, the August 2026 agreement is currently terminable by either party. Neither party has delivered notice of termination as of the date of this prospectus, and we do not currently intend to terminate the agreement."
The company also has contracts with Nscale, Akamai, and CoreWeave.
Anthropic reported a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter, compared to a $974 million operating profit in the quarter prior, which it attributed primarily to such short-term compute deals.
The new filing also lays out Anthropic's expectations for the IPO, with the company stating it plans to offer its Class A common stock at between $70 and $78, targeting a valuation of $1.4trn.

# Energy storage firm Torus launches prefabricated modular data center product, raises $500m

Funding to support scaling of Torus Foundry product

November 12, 2026

By

Zachary Skidmore

Have your say

Utah-based energy storage developer Torus has raised $500 million in Series C funding and launched a modular AI data center product.

– Zachary Skidmore

The $500m raise was led by Magnetar and is expected to support the scaling of the company’s Torus Foundry modular data center solution.
According to the company, Foundry is a prefabricated modular solution with a capacity of 1-20MW per site delivered in shipping-sized containers.
The company said that the units will be installed behind the meter, utilizing headroom at existing transformers, with each unit paired with Torus Reserve, the company's flywheel-and-battery storage system, which it claims can smooth AI inference loads, allowing more capacity to be installed on an existing grid connection, while providing backup power during outages.
The company said that site preparation for the units will take approximately a week, with installation and commissioning taking between one to two days. The full process, from signing the contract to operations, is expected to take between 12 and 16 weeks.
Each of the units is prefabricated at Torus’ 545,000 sq ft (50,630 sqm) factory in Salt Lake City, Utah, and will be vertically integrated, combining power, storage, cooling, networking and compute into one unit. The unit utilizes closed-loop cooling, and because it runs off existing grid capacity, avoids the need to construct new power and generation capacity.
The company said that customers will be able to purchase a powered shell without GPUs, a turnkey bare-metal unit with GPUs, or dedicated single-tenant inference capacity. The first announced customers of the unit are GPU cloud company Hydra Host, as well as another, unnamed, AI cloud provider.
“The industry has been trying to solve AI’s power problem by building net-new infrastructure, which causes costs to potentially rise and takes years to bring compute online,” said Nate Walkingshaw, CEO and founder of Torus. “Inference doesn’t have to wait. We’ve spent years learning how to make the grid more affordable, flexible, resilient, and intelligent, and Foundry applies that to compute: capacity in weeks, with power that’s already available. Most providers are bringing power to the chips. Foundry brings the chips to power.”
The company said that the unit already has thousands of GPUs deployed, and plans to have more than 47,000 GPUs deployed in Foundry units by the end of 2027. It said that the Salt Lake City production facility will be capable of producing 500 MW of IT load, with plans to expand to 1GW in the near future.

# Kraft Group could build 900MW data center campus in Sutton, Massachusetts, investing $16 billion

Property would scale from an initial two buildings to ten by 2033

November 11, 2026

By

Barney Dixon

Have your say

The Kraft Group could build a 900MW data center campus in Sutton, Massachusetts, a local official has revealed.
In a memo to the town's Select Board, Sutton town manager Austin Cyganiewicz revealed that the Robert Kraft-owned conglomerate was planning the development alongside Sutton-based packaging firm Unified Global Packaging Group.

– Sutton town, Massachusetts

The campus would be situated at Unified’s Parkway property, off Boston Road and Providence Road, and would consist of an initial two buildings, with a planned launch in 2029. This initial phase would cover about 250,000 sq ft (23,225 sqm) per building, at roughly 90MW of power capacity each.
Two more buildings would be constructed each year over the next four years, until 2033.
Potential workloads were not disclosed.
The memo said the development would draw around 900MW at full build-out and represent more than $16 billion of private investment, based on estimates from the developer.
According to Cyganiewicz, the assessed value of all property in Sutton currently stands at $2.7 billion.
The memo suggested that property would pay around $10.4 million in property tax each year, once fully assessed in 2031. This would rise to $27.8 million at full build-out.
Cyganiewicz said this would almost match the entire 2027 tax levy of the town, which is projected to be $32 million.
A 2020 US census puts Sutton’s population at just 9,357.
“Because the town raises only what its budget requires, the main effect would be lower tax bills,” Cyganiewicz added, “about $2,300 less for the average single-family home in FY2031 and about $5,800 less in FY2035.”
While these calculations have been made, the proposal remains “tentative,” with a formal application yet to be filed.
Details on power, water, and equipment were still to come, Cyganiewicz said, but discussions are currently underway with the local regional grid operator to secure the necessary power, with reclaimed water used for cooling.
Cyganiewicz outlined a timeline for approval of the project, with community benefits discussions, zoning bylaws, and a technical review all taking place in parallel, culminating in a town meeting and vote in May 2027.
A Select Board meeting took place last night (November 10, 2026) at the Sutton Town Hall. While it was not specifically a public hearing, public comments were welcome at the beginning of the session.
According to social media comments after the meeting, residents raised concerns about the potential noise from an operational data center, as well as a potential moratorium on data centers in the town.
Under an executive order from Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey, data centers over 25MW proposed in the state must be approved by local communities, and developers must implement a community benefits agreement that adheres to specific state standards .

- **Draft and timing:** The CAC opened a consultation on draft Administrative Measures for Digital Virtual Human Information Services on 3 April 2026, and it closed on 6 May 2026 until 6 May 2026. One source calls it the first dedicated governance framework for the sector.
- **Labelling:** Sources describe a requirement that virtual human content carry a prominent disclosure label. Another says providers would have to prominently label services as digital humans.
- **Other provisions:** The draft also covers consent for using someone's likeness, a ban on virtual intimate relationships for minors, and limits on evading identity verification. It is described as a 23-article text.
- **Related earlier rules:** The CAC's separate AI-generated content labelling measures were released for consultation on 14 September 2024 the draft Measures for the Labelling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content. That is a different regime from the digital human draft.

I could not confirm whether the April draft has been finalized or whether a new consultation is planned for November 2026. Any such step would need a fresh search or the CAC's official site to verify.

AUTH: Josip Vrdoljak, Akash Singh, Bas Steunebrink, Alex Yarotsky, John Lorenzo, Achille Nicoletti, Sam Pigott
COM: 17 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Dataset: this https URL ; leaderboard: this https URL
ABS: ExpertCrowd-SWE (EC-SWE) is a benchmark of 100 expert-authored, multi-file software engineering tasks for evaluating autonomous coding agents in large, unfamiliar codebases. Each task is a change request written by a practising engineer against a pinned commit of a real repository, paired with a sealed reference solution and a task-specific grader whose weighted, mostly executable criteria award partial credit; must-pass blockers and pass/fail gates encode what a maintainer would refuse to merge. The tasks span 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. The median ticket is 148 words, while the median reference solution changes 471 lines. Every task image is calibrated before release so that the reference solution scores 1.0 and both the untouched repository and an inert change score 0; nearly half of the tasks also ship alternative, lazy and adversarial control patches that the grader must classify correctly. The final 100 tasks were selected for difficulty against current frontier models. We evaluate seven frontier models, five runs each (3,495 scored runs), in a single platform harness that gives each model its provider-native tool interface. Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3%) and GPT-6 Astra (63.7%) lead without a statistically significant gap, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0%), and a statistically indistinguishable group of Qwen 3.8 Max, DeepSeek V4.1 Flas

### 2611.13355 | DEPUTYBENCH: Evaluating Contextual Safety in Enterprise Agents
AUTH: Hao Zhao, Minghao Lin
COM: 
ABS: Enterprise agents must determine whether ordinary requests are permitted by organizational records and policies while continuing legitimate work. We introduce DEPUTYBENCH, an executable benchmark with 79 base items, 375 instances, paired permission contexts, and graded evidence requirements. Across 12 models, revised audits give 88.0% pooled safety and 79.1% paired success. A controlled study of 28 derived tasks and six models tests authorization-fact flips, evidence masking, and irrelevant rewrites. Outcomes track backend permissions, yet restricted execution is more frequent with missing evidence than explicit non-permission: 10.3% versus 3.5% on 27 matched tasks, a 6.8-percentage-point difference (95% interval: 1.9-13.0; secondary analysis). A post-hoc analysis locates 61 of 100 masked-condition executions in four privacy tasks requiring complete cumulative counts or person-specific consent. The difference persists when the most error-prone model or the largest contributing task is excluded, but is much smaller outside those four tasks. Thus high safety with available evidence does not establish reliable stopping when permission cannot be verified. Mean paired success is equivalent within a prespecified five-point margin under irrelevant rewrites, while strong-model safety remains near ceiling. Scorer validation improves from 178 to 266 correctly scored cases out of 284 held

### 2611.12970 | TrustMod-SM: A Multi-Axis Benchmark for Evaluating Trustworthiness of LLMs in Social Media Content Moderation
AUTH: Aizan Zafar, Sreekantam Sai Venkata, Gathik Jindal, Ritu Raj Sharma, Zishan Ahmad, Tulika Saha, Srinath Srinivasa
COM: 
ABS: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential for social media content moderation, but their trustworthiness beyond overall accuracy remains underexplored. We introduce TrustMod-SM, a benchmark of roughly 29,000 instances across eight datasets, to evaluate LLM moderators on five dimensions: trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity. Evaluating 16 open-weight models (0.5B-284B parameters, spanning text-only and vision-language architectures) and one closed frontier model, we find persistent trustworthiness gaps. Higher detection accuracy often coincides with greater demographic disparity, and models frequently comply with concealment or exaggeration prompts, assign high confidence to wrong predictions, rarely escalate ambiguous cases, and struggle to separate hate speech from counter-speech or reclaimed language (especially below 8B parameters). Scaling does not uniformly resolve these issues, and no single model excels across all five dimensions.

### 2611.13398 | The Dose Makes the Poison: Exposure-Aware Evaluation of Generative Drug Design
AUTH: Maria Franz, N. Benjamin Erichson
COM: 14 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the AI4DD workshop (AI for Drug Discovery: Bridging the Translation Gap), NeurIPS 2026
ABS: Generative models are increasingly used to propose molecules for drug discovery. They can produce far more candidates than can be experimentally tested, making computational selection essential. Most selection methods rely on predicted molecular properties, such as potency and toxicity, but overlook how these properties translate into drug exposure at a given dose. As a result, molecules that appear promising on paper may require impractical doses or raise safety concerns. We investigate this gap by using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations to re-evaluate molecules selected from three PARP1-targeted generative pipelines. Of 60 shortlisted molecules, seven fail to achieve sufficient target exposure, while 28% of the remaining candidates show predicted safety risks at their required dose. Moreover, 85% of candidates with an achievable dose are outperformed by molecules overlooked during static selection. These findings suggest that accounting for dose and exposure can substantially change which generated molecules are considered promising for drug development.

### 2611.14221 | Stagewise and interpretable emergence of inside-outside computation in Transformer-based language models
AUTH: Jack T. Parley
COM: 20 pages, 9 figures
ABS: Variability in syntactic structure and parsing ambiguity are fundamental aspects of natural language which modern LLMs have to learn to deal with proficiently. Previous "post-mortem" studies have shown that fully trained Transformers indeed approximate canonical parsing algorithms such as inside-outside, but little is established theoretically about how this is actually learned. Here, we make a first step towards addressing this by studying the learning dynamics in synthetic context-free grammars with variable parse tree topology. The stagewise learning curves are fully interpretable, in the sense that all of the loss stages a) can be computed analytically, and b) can be clearly associated to the representation of a hidden latent tree variable, which allows to lift ambiguity and utilize information from wider contexts. By probing representations, we visualize the emergence of inside-outside computation across depth and during training: while during early stages local (bigram/trigram) information is used and involves only a few initial layers, gradually the Transformer develops an encoder-decoder structure where the most abstract latent information is encoded in the middle, and the latter half of the network is used to progressively refine the final token prediction. ### 2611.14210 | Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits
AUTH: Hadi Salloum, Ammar Ali
COM: 
ABS: Weight-space programming, introduced in recent MIT work by Takehi et al., enables a frontier LLM agent to read a network's weights and write a repair. Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests. Our method, Tree-Ising, casts this repair as a sparse discrete optimization problem over the model's own BF16 weights. Forward statistics define an objective that weakens a loop direction, strengthens a concluding direction, and preserves the layer's output on productive tokens. Within a state-tree representation, where lossless BF16 storage acts as a special case, the admissible edits are sign flips and exponent shifts that preserve all shared group exponents and mantissas. We decompose this objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems, one per output row, which we solve on a GPU using simulated annealing or quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation. On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported. The simulated bifurcation solver yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%. Both solvers outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K a

### 2611.14320 | Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
AUTH: Yukyeong Lee, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Sung Ju Hwang
COM: Submitted to ACL Rolling Review (October 2026 cycle); under review
ABS: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. ### 2611.13684 | BypassGym: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents' Endpoint Defense Evasion Capabilities
AUTH: Weifeng Yuan, Zifan Chen, Yucheng Zhang, Feng Dong, Peng Gao, Haoyu Wang
COM: 
ABS: Artificial intelligence agents increasingly automate cybersecurity tasks, including offensive operations. Frequent attacks across the web make endpoint detection and response (EDR) a critical defense, but whether AI agents can evade it remains unclear. Benchmarks evaluate the offensive capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents in areas such as penetration testing and vulnerability discovery. One important capability that these benchmarks do not address is defense evasion, specifically whether an agent can develop a program that executes a payload without being blocked or terminated by a deployed EDR. We introduce BypassGym, to our knowledge the first benchmark to systematically evaluate this capability on real endpoints. Given command-and-control (C2) shellcode, an agent must generate and compile a loader that executes the payload without being blocked or terminated. A supplementary evasion knowledge skill provides domain knowledge and supports comparisons with and without this input. BypassGym is built on Proxmox VE(PVE), so the evaluation environment runs real Windows systems and EDR products inside virtual machines and returns structured detection feedback to the agent. We evaluate 5 lightweight model backends against 6 EDR products and 3 payloads, and find that even these simple models generate successful submissions, with DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash reaching 17/18 successf

Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/11/who-runs-the-ransomware-group-qilin/
https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/11/who-runs-the-ransomware-group-qilin/#comments

Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:06:01 +0000

https://krebsonsecurity.com/?p=74550

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub .

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “ Haise ,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP , a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44 .

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

In a new public notice reported by Bloomberg and others, the Starbase City Commission is scheduled to meet on December 9 to consider approval of a property tax abatement agreement with SpaceX. – City of Starbase Elon Musk’s space company is looking to develop a gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility on a 444-acre tract just east of the City of Brownsville, between Boca Chica Blvd and the Port of Brownsville, in Cameron County. SpaceX could invest up to $24 billion in the project, which would be built out in phases and potentially include future expansions. Full details on the scope of the project haven’t been shared. Starbase, formerly Boca Chica Village or Kopernik Shores, is a city in Cameron County, located near the mouth of the Rio Grande River and adjacent to the country’s border with Mexico. Founded in the 1960s, SpaceX chose what was then Boca Chica to host a rocket launch site in 2014. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk announced plans to incorporate a new city to be called Starbase in the area in 2021, with the city officially incorporated in 2025. Many of the city’s ~500 residents are SpaceX employees, and Bobby Peden, a SpaceX vice president, is currently serving as mayor. SpaceX’s data center and AI division, SpaceXAI (aka SpaceXSI), runs a cluster of data centers around Memphis, with one located in Tennessee and the rest over the state border in Mississippi. These facilities are used to run the company’s AI chatbot, Grok, and provide AI cloud services to clients including Anthropic and Google. Musk recently announced two new Mississippi data centers, named Gun Range and Spam. The billionaire claims to have more than 1GW of capacity in the Memphis cluster, though these claims have been disputed . The company is also looking to develop a 6GW cluster in Cochise County, Arizona. Over 35,000 Grok-Built Apps Exposed Online, Some Leaking Confidential Data and Passwords

# Over 35,000 Grok-Built Apps Exposed Online, Some Leaking Confidential Data and Passwords

 Swati Khandelwal  Nov 11, 2026 Artificial Intelligence / Data Security

Of the 37,571 Grok-built apps that security company Claroc found online, 35,578 were open to anyone without a sign-in, the researchers said yesterday.

They included 24 apps built by staff at the social network X and at SpaceXSI, the company that makes the Grok AI assistant. Most of the open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators, but about 1 in 10 contained internal business or personal data.

The staff apps included a confidential onboarding plan for a new sales hire, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential. SpaceXSI, formerly known as xAI, has since taken down all 24 staff apps but not other users' apps, the researchers said.

Besides those staff apps, the open apps contained internal data from 30 other organizations the researchers could identify, across fields ranging from construction and energy to healthcare and defense. Of those, 26 have more than 1,000 employees, and 6 are Fortune 500 companies.

According to the researchers' estimate in their report , roughly 2% of the open apps contained material serious enough to rate as high or critical.

The exposed material included a hospital group's searchable list of more than 3,500 employees, an intensive care briefing on a single patient, a fire department's live shift board, and a contractor's timesheet whose code held every employee's password in plain text.

Grok can build a working app from a description typed into its chat, a feature its maker opened to every Grok plan on August 19. This chat builder shares the Grok Build name with a separate terminal coding tool, whose repository uploads were reported on July 14.

Each published app gets its own subdomain of grok.me, and its creator chooses who can open it, according to the company's launch announcement .

No app goes public until its creator clicks Publish. In the paid account the researchers used, the next step offered 3 access settings: "Anyone with the link", "Invited users" and "Only you". "Anyone with the link" was already selected.

The setting matters because an app's address does not stay secret, the researchers say. Opening an app makes the visitor's computer look up its subdomain in DNS. Passive DNS services record such lookups, and anyone with an account can search those records by pattern.

Grok suggests 4 random words as each app's name, and about half of the names the researchers found followed that pattern. Such names are hard to guess, but that does not protect an app whose name already sits in a searchable list.

ChatGPT's app builder also puts each app on its own subdomain. But when the researchers shared an app there, its access was set to "Only me" until they changed it. A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say.

The researchers found the Grok app names using common subdomain discovery methods and loaded each app's first page once, without signing in.

To see what protection Grok adds on its own, the researchers built 2 test apps with made-up data and published both with the access setting already selected, "Anyone with the link".

The first, a contact list, got a database but no sign-in. Without signing in, the researchers added a row from a private browser window, and the next visitor saw it.

The second, a customer list for a 4-person sales team, got sign-in buttons that Grok added on its own: "Continue with Google" and "Continue with X". But the code Grok wrote added each person who signed in to the team before checking whether they belonged, so the check always passed.

An uninvited Google account belonging to someone other than the owner got in, viewed every customer, edited one record, and deleted another.

The researchers ran these tests only on their own apps. They did not test whether any of the open apps they found would accept such changes.

The researchers reported their findings to SpaceXSI on Sunday through the address in its security.txt file, including 2 of the staff apps. They reported the other 22 on Monday.

By the time the researchers published yesterday, the company had not replied to their report, but it had answered a reporter's questions about the research.

As the researchers describe, the company said Grok apps stay private until their creator shares them. Publishing takes several steps, including choosing between "Only you" and "Anyone with the link," as well as a legal disclaimer. Employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default.

Even so, 24 apps built by staff at the company and at X were open to anyone, the researchers say.

With their report, the researchers had asked the company to make "Only you" the default and to add an option that limits an app to a company's own email domain.

The company's response did not state that it would contact the owners of other open apps, according to the researchers. They have started emailing the affected organizations themselves and had emailed 3 by the time they published. They withheld every app address and title from the report.

On October 18, the same researchers published Muse research showing that pages shared from Meta's Muse AI agent could be found through passive DNS. Meta disabled sharing, then announced a sharing fix on October 22 that gave shared items new addresses.

# How to Check Your Organization's Grok Apps

Claroc, which sells tools to find and secure apps built with AI, recommends these checks:

- Find out which AI app builders your staff uses. Builders such as Grok, Lovable, Replit, v0, Bolt, Base44 and Google AI Studio can be used without IT setting them up or a company account.

- If you have access to passive DNS data, look up the builders' domains and open any results in a private browser window.

- Make sure any Grok app with internal data is set to "Invited users" or "Only you", and that a stranger gets an error page.

- Try to sign in with an account from outside your company. If it gets in, the app needs a list of who is allowed.

- Check the scripts each app loads for names, email addresses and passwords, and unpublish apps that have no owner.

In the researchers' tests, setting an app to "Only you" caused it to return a 401 error to a stranger for both the page and its data, and unpublishing took an app offline within seconds.

AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets

# AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets

 Ravie Lakshmanan  Nov 11, 2026 Artificial Intelligence / Web Security

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a campaign in which an emerging agentic penetration testing platform called AntiFox has been used to steal Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials and pivot laterally into compromised environments.

"In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The activity has been observed chaining together web exploitation and web shell deployment to facilitate configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access, and storage operations.

AntiFox, available for download from GitHub, has been described as an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven autonomous penetration testing platform that's built atop the "solid foundation" of ARTEX . As of writing, the project has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times.

On its README page , the project maintainer states -

Given an authorized target, a planner / worker / main-agent multi-agent system runs the full engagement over a dual-graph core (a global asset graph + a per-task exploration graph) — recon → attack-surface discovery → exploitation → finding capture → report delivery — fully observable, interactive, and deliverable

Unlike most automated pentest tools that are "great at discovery, but stop at discovery," AntiFox puts its weight on delivery — turning what the AI finds into a report that an engineer can understand, reproduce, back with evidence, and hand straight to the client.

According to Arctic Wolf, some of the initial access activity is associated with a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) application. The access is then leveraged to create an ASPX web shell using "w3wp.exe," the IIS worker process, and run operating system commands to perform the following actions -

- Run PowerShell commands to locate web.config files and configuration backups

- Read application settings and database connection strings

- Enumerate debug and error-log directories

- Attempts to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from the application configuration

- Copy configuration and log files into a web-accessible upload directory

"On a compromised IIS server, commands run through w3wp.exe identified the execution context with whoami, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions with icacls, and tested the ability to write files into the web root," Arctic Wolf said.

"The creation of an ASPX web shell by w3wp.exe, followed by command execution through the same IIS worker process, suggests compromise through the affected web application."

The precise vulnerability used to achieve code execution on the IIS server is not known. In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means.

AntiFox Demo

Specifically, this involved abusing valid IAM identities to validate credentials and enumerate dozens of services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock.

While a majority of these authenticated cross-service API requests ended up with an "AccessDenied" error, some of the discovery and secret-access operations were successful, according to the cybersecurity company.

In at least some instances, the activity has been observed progressing beyond Secrets Manager enumeration to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Elsewhere, a valid AWS identity was used for S3 discovery and object operations via API calls.

"Agentic frameworks such as these make penetration testing techniques more accessible to threat actors, while increasing the speed and consistency with which these techniques can be applied in live attacks," Arctic Wolf said.

# The Rise of AI Tools in Cyber Attacks

The disclosure comes as threat actors are increasingly weaponizing AI-powered penetration testing tools like ARTEX to conduct broad-scale attacks across the world, enabling them to automate various stages of an intrusion with minimal human intervention.

The integration of AI has allowed adversaries, both large and small, to adapt established tradecraft and deploy them at machine speed , making it possible to progress from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Earlier this week, VECERT disclosed details of a campaign dubbed Operation Ghost-Campus that uses AI agents to maintain perpetual, cost-free access to large language models (LLMs) and eventually perform automated academic fraud and steal data belonging to over 5,000 students enrolled at the Fengxian Campus. The campaign has been attributed to a Chinese threat actor.

"The agent industrializes the creation of accounts on the search engine fofa.info, scans the global cyberspace for misconfigured servers, extracts API keys for OpenAI and DeepSeek, automatically verifies their financial balances, and injects them into the attacker's development environment," VECERT said .

"This stolen computing power fuels an interactive GoTTY terminal ('Pi — AI Coding Assistant') and, by extension, provides intelligence to the scripts that sustain academic fraud bots ('heartbeat' bots) and extractors of financial data and personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to thousands of students at the Fengxian Campus."

According to data from Censys, there are 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026, with most of them located in the U.S., Hong Kong, China, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea. However, it's worth noting that not every instance is necessarily malicious in nature.

In a separate report, Check Point Research said it identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances exposing their full databases.

"In many observed cases, ARTEX required remarkably little interaction from its operators once an objective had been established," Check Point said . "Rather than continuously directing attacks step by step, operators frequently issued a goal and left the agent fleet to work toward it. Human interactions were largely limited to checking progress, asking whether a target had been compromised or occasionally adjusting priorities."

The vast majority of the attacks are designed to siphon cryptocurrency, steal Apple code-signing certificates, compromise gaming accounts, and conduct denial-of-service (DoS) attacks against gambling websites. The activity has been found to exploit vulnerabilities related to weak or hard-coded passwords, missing authentication, insecure direct object references, and remote code execution.

In the campaign targeting Apple code-signing certificates, ARTEX agents searched compromised systems for certificate databases, followed by validating the stolen certificates by checking passwords, private keys, Apple revocation status, expiration dates, and associated provisioning profiles.

results:
I couldn't find any Epoch AI analysis dated November 11, 2026. The most recent Epoch-authored items I found are from September 2026 or earlier.

- **September 2026:** Epoch's Data Insights reported that acknowledgments of AI use in arXiv math preprints rose from 4% in April 2026 to 25% in August. A separate Epoch/Ipsos poll found that the share of US adults using AI at least 6 days a week rose from 8% in March 2026 to 19% in August 2026.
- **June 2026:** Epoch launched MirrorCode, a new long-horizon coding benchmark, co-developed with METR.
- **July 2026:** Epoch published a Gradient Update arguing that these claims often rest solely on AI models advancing in capability, and lack serious analysis of just how hard futuristic tech is to build.

Several results from techjacksolutions.com contain benchmark tables and model names that I couldn't verify against Epoch's own site, so I wouldn't rely on them. For anything from November 2026, check epoch.ai directly, especially its Data Insights page.

# Investigating vault particles with Claude
We’re sharing another finding from Anthropic’s biology research lab: the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells. Here, we describe how Claude helped at each step of this research.

# AI for scientific discovery: How researchers use Claude
We analyzed 207,000 research sessions to learn how Claude is used in science, why some tasks get more use than others, and how AI could speed up discovery.

# How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
As AI does more of the hands-on work, the hope is that experts still make the judgment calls, meaning the decisions with more than one defensible answer. We tested this with 50 professional analysts who did a statistical analysis with Claude Code. On each key decision, we randomly assigned which of two defensible options the agent would favor. Analysts mostly went with the agent’s side, and few named the agent as a reason afterward.

# Illuminating the frontier
Anthropic is sharing new measurements that would give the public visibility into frontier AI development.

# Scenarios for our economic future
Anthropic’s Economics team is sharing a new model of how AI may affect economic growth, jobs, wages, and more by 2030. The model lets you explore the scenarios, tell us what you think will happen, and see how your answers compare to +10,000 Americans.

- **Into the Unknown:** One benchmark asks AI agents to write follow-up papers on open problems from US Department of Energy labs. results:
I found no announcement of an "AlphaGenome 2" or any DNA methylation feature in these results, so I can't give a date for one.

What the results do show is the original AlphaGenome. Google DeepMind introduced it on June 25, 2025. It is a new AI tool that can comprehensively predict how mutations or variants in human DNA sequences impact gene regulation. A later write-up says DeepMind released AlphaGenome on January 28, with the model published in Nature and detailed on the DeepMind blog. A Nordic Life Science article is dated February 3, 2026.

On methylation specifically, the coverage I found lists other regulatory readouts. One article says the model predicts thousands of functional genomic readouts at single-base resolution, across 11 assay modalities including gene expression, chromatin accessibility, histone marks, transcription factor. The snippet is cut off there, so I can't confirm whether methylation is among the modalities.

To check for a successor model, I'd look for DeepMind's own blog or the Nature paper, since these results are secondary coverage.
