=== investigating-vault-particles-with-claude
HTTP 200 · https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-vault-particles-with-claude · text/html
Investigating vault particles with Claude \ Anthropic
Skip to main content

# 01 A vault-like structure in prokaryotes

We’re sharing another finding from Anthropic’s biology research lab : the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells. Vaults are large, hollow barrels of protein found in cells across the tree of life, and their function is still unknown. Below, we describe how Claude helped at each step of this research: searching across sequence literature, optimizing a method of isolating particles, and mapping the vault’s structure. More information is in our preprint , which we’ve submitted to bioRxiv; we’ll update the link as soon as it goes live.

Biological cells were first detected in 1665, but more than three and a half centuries later, much of how they work remains unknown. Until relatively recently, the existence of some crucial components , let alone their function , was controversial. Even today, more than a third of the roughly 4,400 genes in one of the most comprehensively studied cells, the bacterium E. coli , remain poorly understood . Another such enigma is the vault particle .
A vault particle is a large, hollow protein shell found in nearly all the cells in our body. It was discovered in 1986 by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha, but its function remains elusive. At roughly three times the mass of a ribosome, it’s one of the largest known molecular complexes in eukaryotes—organisms with complex cells, such as mammals (as opposed to simple, usually single-celled “prokaryotes,” such as bacteria). Vaults take their name from their shape. When observed under an electron microscope, the ribbed shell reminded Dr. Rome and Dr. Kedersha of the vaulted ceiling of a cathedral. In mammals, the shell is made of 78 copies of the major vault protein, arranged as two identical halves joined at the middle.
Vaults are found across most of the eukaryotic tree , from slime molds to humans, so scientists believe that they must do something useful. Researchers have proposed various functions, including transporting molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm , protecting cells from toxic compounds such as cancer drugs , and supporting innate immunity , but none of these proposals have been conclusively confirmed. Other studies have shown that mice lacking vaults still survive , which suggests that vaults may be necessary only under specific environmental conditions. Still, the question remains: why would evolution retain something so large if it didn’t have an important function?
Interested in whether Claude could help make progress on this long-standing open problem, our biology research team has been investigating vaults. We haven’t yet determined their biological function, but we did find that many more vault proteins across the tree of life, including those in prokaryotes and the bacteriophages that infect them, can assemble into complete vault-like particles. Related proteins had already been found in the genomes of both prokaryotes and phages, but to our knowledge no one had shown that they assemble into vaults.
A vault in a prokaryotic cell gives researchers a simpler system to study. Compared with mammalian cells, bacteria are quick to grow, which makes it easier to investigate where vaults came from, what their basic structure looks like, and what, if anything, they contain. Studying the bacterial relatives of human proteins has been informative before. Bacterial versions of cGAS–STING signaling , gasdermins , and viperins revealed the microbial origins of these human immune defenses. In those cases, their function in humans was already known. For vaults it is not, and their prokaryotic relatives may help reveal it.
Here, we describe how we uncovered the molecular structure of a vault from a bacteriophage . Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. Like all viruses, they hijack their host cells to make their proteins, so this vault would be built inside a bacterium, a prokaryotic cell. The vault is built from 96 copies of a single protein, compared with 78 in human vaults. By duplicating part of the protein, we engineered the vault to be even larger. Together, these results shed light on how such complexes assemble and suggest how they could be adapted for biotechnology —for example, as nanocapsules for delivering enzymes .

=== how-researchers-use-claude
HTTP 200 · https://www.anthropic.com/research/how-researchers-use-claude · text/html
How scientists use Claude \ Anthropic
Skip to main content

# 01 Summary

Johannes Hermle*, Ben Jones*, Lukas Althoff*, Ryan Heller, Thomas Lyttelton, Carolyn Stein, Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
*Lead authors of the report

# Summary

- What we measure. AI could speed up scientific discovery, but by how much depends on what AI can do and how scientists use it. Using privacy-preserving methods, we study 207,000 Claude and Claude Code research sessions to understand how Claude is used across scientific fields and research tasks. We are conducting this research to help the public better understand the state of AI for science today and assess the impact that AI may have on scientific discovery in the future.

- Where scientists use Claude. Relative to the number of researchers in each field, Claude is used more in the formal sciences, such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics, and less in health and lab-based physical sciences. Scientists primarily use Claude to analyze data and to write. Data analysis alone accounts for about one-third of sessions on Claude and nearly half of sessions on Claude Code. Scientists use it less for idea generation and data gathering, even though, in an accompanying survey, they rank those tasks as the most important for scientific discovery. That said, specialized AI tools designed for scientific work could narrow the gap between the research tasks scientists use AI for and the ones they consider most important. On Claude Science, for instance, idea generation makes up about twice the share of use that it does on Claude.

=== agents-judgment-calls
HTTP 200 · https://www.anthropic.com/research/agents-judgment-calls · text/html
How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls \ Anthropic
Skip to main content

# 01 Study design

Amaç Herdağdelen, Hailey Joren, Alex Tamkin
When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call.
We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded.
Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead.
Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed.
Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment.
Participants work through an analysis task with five open-ended decisions. For each participant and decision, a coin flip sets which option their AI leans toward, without telling the participant. We compare how often participants choose option A under each lean.


=== investigating-unintended-model-actions
HTTP 200 · https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions · text/html
Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
This report describes examples of unintended model actions we’ve observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude. It is part of our effort to publish more frequent standalone reports on model behavior and alignment beyond our system cards, which we publish with each model release, and our risk reports, which we publish every three to six months as part of our Responsible Scaling Policy. We believe it’s important to be transparent about what we see our models do during testing and use.
The behaviors can be grouped into four categories:

- Claude exploiting a basic flaw in software to run commands on a server;

- Claude submitting a sensitive form on a real website when it should not have;

- Claude working around a restriction to reach data that was gated by a token or a fee; and

- Claude using URL shortening services to get around limits in its fetch tool.
We have chosen not to name the organizations involved in the examples below to avoid exposing vulnerabilities in their systems, and at their request. For this reason, we also provide less detail about each case than we otherwise would. Some of the cases described below involved websites run by U.S. government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels. We have briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved.

=== alignment-assessment-ukaisi
HTTP 200 · https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-ukaisi · text/html
An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident \ Anthropic
Skip to main content

# 01 Alignment assessment summary

On August 4, 2026, the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) published a report that detailed some concerning behavior it observed from Claude Mythos 5 during its testing of the model’s cyber capabilities. In AISI’s evaluation, Mythos 5 was given a capture-the-flag (CTF) cybersecurity challenge, in which it was asked to retrieve a protected piece of data (the “flag”) from a simulated network. Internet access was deliberately enabled (this was standard for AISI’s cyber testing at the time, but is no longer). The cyber safeguards we deploy with general release models like Fable 5 were disabled. In nine of AISI’s 43 evaluation runs, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions (i.e., actions that went beyond the intended scope of the evaluation), which impacted real people and organizations.
In this post, which is being published alongside an independent report from AISI, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment. Like AISI’s report, we concentrate on the transcript (the complete record of the model’s reasoning and actions) from a single evaluation run. In this run:

- To capture the flag, Claude Mythos 5 was tasked with breaking into a small network of computers that AISI had built for the test, designed to resemble a real organization’s systems.

- It attempted—unsuccessfully—a range of approaches that targeted these systems using the methods that the evaluation intended.

- However, it also quickly found evidence that one of these machines periodically contacted GitHub, which hosts code repositories.

- **Microsoft "Lazarus" research:** Microsoft researchers showed that an AI model can be given a hidden backdoor by changing a small number of neurons, without retraining (fewer than 10 of its rarely used neurons). One example describes an agent that begins emitting a download-and-execute command after its context indicates the calendar has crossed into 2027. Sources disagree on the count: one CSA briefing says editing seven neurons can turn an open-weight agent model into a shell-command backdoor.

A DEV Community post cites an AE Studio experiment, reported November 11, in which agents fixing a service had to guard a secret token.

The WIU page carries an "84 days ago" age tag despite listing November 11 items, and the CSA pages are briefing summaries rather than primary sources. # Frontier Ready Daily – 11 November 2026

CSAI Foundation Initiative

# Frontier Ready Daily

Machine-speed agentic cybersecurity — the top news for enterprises building toward it.

Issue 77

Date 11 November 2026

Items 6

Significance 3 major · 3 notable

Download this issue as PDF

Prototype. Frontier Ready Daily is an early-stage feed published automatically each morning. Items are selected and drafted by an automated research pipeline against a published editorial standard, and are machine-validated for provenance, source quality and vendor neutrality before release — but each issue is published without prior human review. Treat items as leads to verify at the linked source rather than as finished CSA research. Corrections: [email redacted] .

# In this issue

An AI-assisted researcher published working exploits for more than 30 N-central flaws without notifying N-able, and the vendor took its hosted remote-management platform offline the next day and shipped a partial hotfix within two days. Railway's final report on its October breach says the attacker used agents and reached KMS decryption of customer secrets nearly 15 hours after its first alert, and the stolen AI keys ran up an estimated $740,000 that Railway will cover where providers will not refund. The other items cover Fireworks AI's widened breach, which was a second intrusion through a third-party cloud provider 17 days after the first; NEAR AI's confirmation that its enclave did not protect requests from a flaw in the inference engine running inside it; more than 35,000 Grok-built apps open to anyone without sign-in because the publish step preselected "Anyone with the link"; and Microsoft's November patch release, which takes its 2026 total past 5,100 fixes. We examined Microsoft's "Lazarus" research, which shows open-weight agent models can be backdoored by editing fewer than 10 neurons, and left it out of the items because it is a laboratory demonstration and Microsoft has not seen it used in the wild. CSA's note Seven Neurons to Root: Lazarus Weight-Edit Backdoors in Agent Models covers it.

# Today’s Items

1

# An AI-assisted researcher dropped working exploits for 30-plus N-central flaws without notice, and N-able pulled its hosted platform offline within a day and shipped a partial fix in two

major vuln_storm VERBATIM (PROVIDER) for N-able's takedown, its on-premises shutdown advice, the seven CVEs fixed in 2026.4 HF2, and its statement that it has not observed exploitation; LINK ONLY — VERIFY AT SOURCE for the researcher's account of AI-assisted discovery and of earlier reports that went unanswered for five to six months, which N-able did not address; SELF-REPORTED (PROVIDER METRIC) for Defused's report of scanning and Shadowserver's fall in exposed servers from about 1,338 to about 148; CHARACTERIZATION (CSA) for reading this as a disclosure-process failure that turned AI discovery speed into an outage

What changed

Late on 8 November 2026, researcher Sean Bales published the "Able2Shell" repository, with proof-of-concept exploits for more than 30 alleged flaws in N-able's N-central remote monitoring and management platform. He told BleepingComputer the discovery was AI-assisted. He did not notify N-able, saying flaws he had reported in another N-able product five to six months earlier were still unpatched. On 9 November N-able took hosted N-central offline in all regions and told on-premises customers to shut their servers down. On 10 November it released 2026.4 HF2, which N-able says fixes "some" of the flaws, including seven CVEs it calls the most critical, and reported all hosted servers upgraded. Defused observed attackers probing N-central for the flaws the same day. Exposed servers counted by Shadowserver fell from about 1,338 to about 148.

Why it reaches you

The component is the RMM platform, which holds remote-execution rights over every managed endpoint, often through a managed service provider you do not operate. The time from public exploit to vendor fix was about two days, but the time from public exploit to probing was also about two days, and the service was unavailable in between. The hotfix does not cover every published flaw. A single researcher's AI-assisted output forced a vendor-wide outage, and the trigger was a stalled disclosure channel, not the volume of findings alone.

What to do escalate

IT operations owner, with the MSP relationship owner: escalate. Confirm every N-central instance, including any your MSP runs for you, is on 2026.4 HF2 or later and is not reachable from the internet. Ask the MSP in writing which of the published flaws remain unfixed and what compensating controls are in place until they are. Add to RMM supplier reviews a question on how the vendor handles reports it has not yet triaged. Urgency: escalate.

Source: BleepingComputer — N-able releases security hotfixes for zero-day vulnerabilities

CSA coverage: Able2Shell: N-central Zero-Days and the RMM Kill Switch ; see also When Discovery Outruns Remediation: Open-Source Disclosure Strain .

2

# Railway says an agent-driven attacker reached KMS decryption of customer secrets nearly 15 hours after its first alert, and the stolen AI keys ran up an estimated $740,000 that Railway will cover where providers refuse

major machine_speed VERBATIM (PROVIDER) for Railway's timeline, its description of the attack as "a contest of agent speed" with "agent fanouts" and "abliterated models with no safeguards", and its refund positions by provider; SELF-REPORTED (PROVIDER METRIC) for the ~$740,000 estimate, the upper bound of about 100,000 workspaces (1.85%), and 1,852 exposed linked-account tokens; CHARACTERIZATION (CSA) for the reading that detection without automated containment did not stop decryption

What changed

On 10 November 2026 Railway published its final report on the October breach of its build infrastructure. The attacker escaped build isolation at 07:28 UTC on 20 October. Railway's on-call engineer was paged at 13:58, about six and a half hours later. The attacker then exploited a misconfigured OIDC binding at 03:26 on 21 October, began decrypting customer environment variables through a machine with KMS access at 04:42, and searched them for AI-provider key names. The attacker was evicted at 09:24, about 26 hours after entry and about 19.5 hours after the alert. Railway's preliminary report of 22 October had dated the start of the attack to the alert and placed decryption later than the final report does. Railway estimates unauthorized spend on the stolen keys at about $740,000. It says AWS Bedrock and Google Gemini are refunding under fraud policies, OpenAI and SpaceXSI are reviewing case by case, OpenRouter will not refund, and Railway will cover OpenRouter and, for now, Anthropic charges itself.

Why it reaches you

The exposure path is any platform-as-a-service or CI host where you store AI-provider keys as environment variables. The decryption that mattered happened nearly 15 hours after Railway's responders were already engaged, so detection alone did not protect customer secrets. Who absorbs the loss depended on each AI provider's refund terms, not on your contract with the platform. Railway's changes are ephemeral per-build VMs, scoped push credentials, just-in-time service credentials, and audit logging on every encrypt and decrypt operation. They give a concrete checklist to ask your own hosts about.

What to do validate

Cloud platform owner, with procurement: validate. For each PaaS and CI provider that holds your AI keys, find out whether decrypt operations on your secrets are logged and visible to you. Move AI keys to per-workload, spend-capped credentials issued by the provider, and record each AI provider's refund position for fraudulent use before you need it. Urgency: validate.

Source: Railway — Incident report: October security incident

CSA coverage: Who Pays for Stolen Inference? Loss Allocation After Black October ; see also Black October: AI Developer Platform Breaches and Industrialized LLMjacking .

3

# NEAR AI says its enclave did not protect requests from an exploited flaw in the SGLang inference engine running inside it

major agentic_surface VERBATIM (PROVIDER) for NEAR AI's statement that confidential computing "does not protect against a vulnerability in the software running inside the environment", and for the impact figures (about 100 users' account details, 18 legacy agents' chat history, settings and logs, two customers' API keys); NO PROVIDER CLAIM on the CVE, the affected SGLang versions, the dates of exploitation and detection, or whether the SGLang project has released a fix; CHARACTERIZATION (CSA) for the procurement implication

What changed

On 9 November 2026 NEAR AI reported that an attacker used a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, the open-source inference engine, to run code on one of its inference servers. That server processes confidential-mode requests inside a trusted execution environment, and NEAR AI says the attacker could have seen requests on it on 8 November, including confidential ones. The attacker also moved beyond the server, reaching account details for about 100 users and the chat history, settings and logs of 18 agents on a legacy deployment that did not run in the enclave. NEAR AI rotated credentials, replaced all agent tokens, deployed a fix across its inference servers, and reported the flaw to SGLang. It has not named a CVE or affected versions.

Why it reaches you

The component is the confidential-inference endpoint and the model-serving stack behind it, whether you buy it as a service or run SGLang and similar engines yourself. Remote attestation proves which code is loaded in the enclave. It does not prove that the code is free of exploitable flaws, and the enclave makes those flaws harder for the operator to see. An enterprise that accepted "runs in a TEE" as its confidentiality control for sensitive prompts or agent traffic has relied on a control that did not hold in this deployed case.

What to do validate

AI platform owner: validate. For every confidential-inference service you use, ask the provider which inference engine and version runs inside the enclave, how quickly it patches that engine, and how it monitors for compromise inside the enclave. If you run SGLang yourself, track the upstream advisory and keep inference servers off the internet until a fixed version is identified. Urgency: validate.

Source: NEAR AI — Security incident report: SGLang vulnerability

CSA coverage: Inside the Enclave, Still Exposed: The NEAR AI SGLang Breach .

results:
The Information reported that the Commerce Department is drafting a rule to stop Chinese AI firms from renting Nvidia GPU compute through data centers in third countries such as Thailand and Singapore. A draft could reach trade groups as early as September. The rule would target remote access through Thailand and Singapore, which aren't subject to the same export controls as China.

The main obstacle is legal authority. Export-control lawyers say BIS lacks statutory authority to police remote access until the Senate passes the Remote Access Security Act. An attorney at Baker McKenzie told The Information that the view that Commerce cannot enforce such a rule under existing law is 'widely acknowledged' within the export-control bar. Commerce could instead use know-your-customer checks, though the Trump administration rescinded the wider AI Diffusion framework in May 2025 and has said it won't enforce that diligence rule.

Separately, on May 31, 2026, Commerce issued guidance that requires licenses for advanced AI chip sales to China-headquartered firms located abroad. The practical effect is to extend existing chip export controls to overseas subsidiaries of Chinese AI firms, including those based in locations such as Malaysia. The loophole traces back to May 2025, when the Trump administration announced it would not enforce the AI Diffusion rule.

I found no result confirming that the remote-access rule has been finalized, so its status is unverified as of today.

# The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning

October 27, 2026
Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni, Google Research

We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs.

Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.
While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting , a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.
Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a sleep framework in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous periodic lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning.

# Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases
Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information.
Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states:

- Active (wake) phase : The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components.

Heart disease, kidney conditions, and metabolic disorders like type 2 diabetes aren't isolated, they form an interconnected web known as cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome . CKM progression often begins silently years before symptoms appear, shaped by everyday habits like movement, sleep, and cardiovascular activity. Catching these subtle shifts early offers the best chance to reverse the trend . Yet while smartwatches easily track what we did yesterday, moving from passive tracking to meaningful action is much harder: How do my daily habits affect my CKM right now? And if I sleep 30 minutes longer or add a brisk walk to my routine, how much will my health improve over the next three months?
Age is often seen as playing a part in answering these questions, but chronological age alone isn’t enough because two people born in the same year can have vastly different physiological health. While researchers have developed “biological clocks ” from blood tests or wearable sensors to estimate whether someone's body is aging faster or slower than their calendar age, most existing clocks aren't built for everyday coaching. Many are trained simply to estimate the birth year, latching onto traits you can't easily change, or act as black boxes that can't show how modifying a specific habit will shift your future health.
In “Personalized health coaching via coachable health age and counterfactual wearable trajectories ” and our companion study, “Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Health Age Using Wearables and Blood Biomarkers ”, we introduce an investigational framework designed to close the loop between tracking a person’s health and actively improving it. The framework provides the following:

- A coachable health age model: An interpretable health-age metric built entirely from modifiable daily behaviors and physiology captured passively by consumer wearables.

- A sensor world model and counterfactual coaching system: A machine learning world model (SensorWM) trained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of wearable data that simulates personalized 12-week "what-if" health trajectories, paired with a language model agent that turns those simulations into realistic, clinician-vetted coaching plans.

- Expansion to multi-organ CKM health: When routine blood tests are available, our framework can be expanded to combine wearable streams with lab biomarkers to detect early, subclinical strain across the heart, kidney, and metabolic systems.

Overview of our framework, from estimating coachable health age and predicting long-term disease risk to simulating 12-week "what-if" habit trajectories for personalized coaching.

# A health age metric you can actually move
To make a health metric useful for coaching, every input should be something that can be tracked continuously and influenced through daily choices. Rather than training a model to guess a person’s birth year, we grounded our coachable health age (CHA) model in published epidemiological studies linking everyday behaviors to cardio-metabolic disease risk. CHA integrates four core signals passively measured by consumer wearables — resting heart rate , daily step count , sleep duration , and weekly Active Zone Minutes — alongside optional markers like VO2max, sleep schedule regularity , and insulin resistance , when available. Because active people often have lower resting heart rates and better sleep, we mathematically adjust for overlap across these signals so each habit contributes its distinct share to your health age delta , the difference between your CHA and chronological age. A negative delta (say, −3 years) means an individual's physiological profile appears younger than their chronological age, while a positive delta signals accelerated aging.
We validated this model across three independent cohorts:

- Predicting future disease ( All of Us research program , n = 22,748): Across more than 68,000 person-years of consenting Fitbit and electronic health record follow-up, healthy participants who had a health age older than their calendar age at baseline were significantly more likely to develop hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or type 2 diabetes over the next eight years. Adding CHA to standard clinical metrics (age, sex, and BMI) significantly improved disease risk prediction, especially among adults under 50.

- Improvement over time (longitudinal Fitbit cohort, n = 1,464): Tracking users across consecutive 3-month windows over two years showed that among users with a sustained change in habits, the CHA decreased.

- Alignment with clinical health ( WEAR-ME study ): Unlike wearable aging clocks trained to predict chronological age, CHA aligned better with the modified American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 cardiovascular score and metabolic syndrome severity score , as well as participants' own self-reported health.

Across 18,423 disease-free participants in the All of Us cohort, those with a health age younger than or equal to their calendar age had significantly higher disease-free survival over 8 years ( left ), while 2-year longitudinal tracking shows that individuals can meaningfully lower their health age over 3-month windows ( right ).

# Playing out "what-if" futures with a sensor world model
Knowing your health age tells you where you stand today. Turning that number into a personalized plan requires answering a "what-if" (or counterfactual) question: What will happen to my body over the next 12 weeks if I change specific habits, and which plan can I realistically stick with?
Simply plugging new step or sleep targets into a static calculator misses how the body adapts as a connected system. When you consistently move more and sleep better over several weeks, your resting heart rate and heart rate variability gradually improve too, creating extra health benefits downstream.
To capture these dynamics, we developed Sensor World Model (SensorWM), an action-conditioned world model pre-trained on 2.28 million person-weeks of de-identified data from roughly 100,000 consenting Fitbit users. Given two weeks of baseline wearable data, SensorWM forecasts how 20 physiological markers will evolve over the next 12 weeks under different daily steps, sleep, and cardio routines, outperforming general-purpose time-series foundation models like TimesFM while preserving the clinical patterns associated with diabetes, hypertension, and insulin resistance.
We paired SensorWM with a feasibility-constrained optimizer and a language model coaching agent to do three things:

- Simulate: SensorWM rolls out 125 candidate 12-week habit combinations for each person, comparing them against a "status-quo" projection if habits stay the same.

- Filter for realism and safety: The most aggressive workout plan doesn't help if it causes burnout in week two. Our optimizer weighs projected health-age reductions against each person's historical habit flexibility and clinical safety bounds, picking a more ambitious target (−2.3 years) for someone with high baseline flexibility, and a gentler ramp (−1.3 years) for someone whose routine is more constrained.

- Coach: The language model translates the top-ranked pathways into a supportive, progressive 12-week coaching plan.

SensorWM simulates 12-week physiological responses under candidate habit changes and balances health-age improvement against each person's historical habit flexibility.

# Put to the test by lifestyle coaches and clinicians

Does grounding a language model in world-model simulations actually produce better guidance than giving the exact same model a user's wearable history alone?
We ran a blinded, head-to-head study with five certified lifestyle coaches and five board-certified primary care and lifestyle medicine physicians across 49 participant profiles spanning five behavioral personas (490 paired reviews total), alongside automated evaluations across the full WEAR-ME cohort ( n = 2,780).

- Strong expert preference: Lifestyle coaches chose the counterfactual-grounded plan as the best overall plan in 71.4% of evaluations (p < 0.001) and rated it more likely to drive long-term adherence in 71.0% of evaluations (p < 0.001).

- Clinician-verified safety: Physicians rated 99.2% of counterfactual plans within safe exercise intensity limits and 97.6% accurate on physiological claims.

- Why it worked: Both coaches and clinicians highlighted that showing people a concrete contrast between their "status-quo" trajectory and achievable "what-if" options (92% vs. 8% among clinicians) gave them a clear, motivating reason to act and a stronger sense of agency (97% vs. 59%).

In blinded evaluations by certified lifestyle coaches and board-certified clinicians, counterfactual-grounded coaching plans were preferred nearly 3-to-1 over generic wearable-grounded plans while meeting 99.2% clinical safety standards.

# Zooming in on organ systems: Adding routine blood biomarkers for CKM health
Because our health age model is modular, it can easily incorporate routine clinical lab tests when available. In our companion study , we expanded the framework to profile CKM syndrome across individual organ systems, pairing continuous wearables with occasional blood biomarkers that alone miss day to day lifestyle patterns.

Conceptual framework of the multimodal CKM health age model, integrating wearable physiology with organ-specific blood biomarkers across diverse aging profiles.

Early CKM decline rarely causes symptoms, and occasional clinic blood draws miss day-to-day lifestyle patterns. Evaluated in 819 WEAR-ME participants, our multimodal CKM health age model combines continuous wearable signals (resting heart rate, steps, active zone minutes, and sleep) with three routine blood biomarkers: cholesterol-to-HDL ratio (cardiovascular), eGFR (kidney filtration), and HOMA-IR (metabolic insulin resistance).
By measuring how far each marker departs from healthy clinical thresholds (a normalized deviance score), the CKM model revealed that multi-organ aging doesn't follow a single template: while metabolic and cardiovascular strain are often correlated, early kidney decline frequently appears independently. Moreover, the resulting CKM health age gap aligned closely with both objective clinical scores (modified Life's Essential 8 r = −0.58; metabolic syndrome severity r = 0.65) and how healthy participants felt day to day.

Population-level heterogeneity across kidney, metabolic, and cardiovascular systems (teal = healthier than reference; brown = subclinical strain), showing why personalized multi-organ profiling matters.

# Looking ahead
Together, these studies show how consumer wearables and machine learning can help shift personal health from looking in the rearview mirror to navigating the road ahead. While our evaluations were conducted offline using retrospective research cohorts, and these models are investigational research prototypes rather than clinical diagnostic tools, they lay the foundation for future prospective trials testing how interactive "what-if" coaching can help people build lasting habits and improve their long-term health.

# Acknowledgements
The research described here is joint work across Google Research and partnering teams. Contributors include Zeinab Esmaeilpour, Simon A. NATO taps Ukraine as red-team in drills to 'trigger an adaptation cycle' - Breaking Defense







A serviceman stands next to the Barracuda drone boat during trials in southern Ukraine, on March 30, 2026. Nina Liashonok/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

MILAN — As NATO races to update its battlefield tactics, a senior official said the use of Ukrainian forces as a “red team” in exercises is meant to “trigger an adaptation cycle” within the alliance.

“My job is to build the capabilities of victory. What we’ve done so far, we took some experience from Ukraine, for example, where we hid some Ukrainian forces and Ukrainian-made USVs and made them the red team against the blue force of NATO,” Adm. Pierre Vandier , Supreme Allied Commander of NATO’s Allied Command Transformation (ACT), told Breaking Defense on Monday.

Vandier didn’t point to any specific exercises, but Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has said that in 2025’s REPMUS exercises off Portugal, Kyiv’s “red team” forces defeated NATO members at sea in five out of five combat scenarios, reportedly in part using unmanned surface vessels.

The threat from unmanned surface vessels has not escaped Vandier . In the current security landscape, he said , if a military were to conduct amphibious operations, it would be equally threatened by naval and aerial drones. “So you cannot envisage any kind of operations without counter-drone [defenses]” and must be able to counter incoming swarms of them.

NATO is also preparing for the modern fight through an initiative called Fight Club within its Joint Warfare Centre. Fight Club is part of a larger five-year campaign and is envisioned as a strategic debate forum that brings together external experts and NATO personnel.

Within Fight Club, Vandier said NATO makes “military vignettes,” essentially focused hypothetical scenarios used to test operational concepts and doctrine to “see where the limit is” in a military concept. “To see,” for instance, “how many drones as part of a swarm will submerge a navy, where is the known limit to trigger adaptation,” he said.

# Assessing The Russian Naval Posture

Last month, another NATO official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Breaking Defense that the alliance has tracked a significant decline in Russian naval presence in the Mediterranean. Until early September, Moscow observed a two-month naval hiatus in the strategic body of water.

However, as Ukraine heads into its fifth winter at war, Vandier said the Russians have been able to sustain momentum in undersea warfare capabilities.

“If you consider the anti-submarine domain, I think the Russians have kept pace in building some good capabilities, like the Yasen-class [advanced nuclear-powered attack submarines], which are good submarines,” Vandier said.

He added that the anti-submarine warfare domain is one of the “main domains of concern” for the alliance.

response.stdout:
Audrey Huang, Nan Jiang, Sham M. Kakade, Sadhika Malladi, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Dylan J. Foster
Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
141 pages including appendices, 3 figures
Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.
---

- **Origin:** MAMUBench was introduced alongside "Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams", by Sahan Paliskara, Nattaput Namchittai, and Andrew Lampinen (arXiv:2610.00583). One news article attributes the paper to Stanford, but I couldn't confirm that affiliation from the other results.
- **Contents:** The authors say they will release the API key, clinic, and personal assistant environments as MAMUBench, comprising 74 scenarios for evaluating multi-user, multi-agent coordination. The paper compares a single coordinator agent serving all users against a team of per-user agents, across five frontier models and 77 scenarios in four environments.
- **Findings:** Per one report, teams of agents underperformed the single coordinator when they shared limited resources, and in the personal-assistant environment coordinators fulfilled targeted requests about twice as often (single-agent coordinators fulfilled targeted user requests twice as often as multi-agent teams).
- **Anthropic link:** The only Anthropic material in the results is a separate multi-agent study from its Frontier Red Team (investigated the behavior of AI agents operating in multiagent environments). It is not MAMUBench.
- **Don't confuse with:** MUMBench, a different multi-user memory benchmark from a Microsoft-affiliated paper on the AIM framework.

The results are secondary coverage and an arXiv abstract, so check the paper directly before relying on these details.

response.result:
**Project Glasswing and VulnCheck findings (Infosecurity Magazine, 11 November 2026)**

**Glasswing overview**
- Project Glasswing is Anthropic's flagship effort to give security researchers its frontier AI models for finding and remediating software vulnerabilities.
- Seven months in, VulnCheck's Patrick Garrity described the project as "overwhelming" maintainers with "underwhelming findings." His report was published November 9.
- Anthropic's coordinated disclosure dashboard, dated November 2, 2026, says Glasswing enabled researchers to find 37,966 vulnerabilities.

**VulnCheck analysis (Garrity)**
- Only 7,349 (19.4%) of those are in Anthropic's public ledger.
- Of the ledger entries, 5,276 were validated as unique vulnerabilities, 1,654 were duplicates, and 419 were withdrawn.
- 4,866 of the validated vulnerabilities have been reported to maintainers, and 193 are in "pre-disclosure."
- 217 have been fixed. The article puts this at "less than 0.5%" of the 37,966 claimed, though 217 out of 37,966 is about 0.57%.
- Between September and November, Anthropic added 4,613 findings to the ledger, but only 15 were marked fixed. 1,668 of the findings added in that period were marked as duplicates.
- Garrity questioned Anthropic's latest claimed 94.2% true positive rate, saying it raises questions about how duplicates and withdrawn findings are counted.
- Garrity concluded: "The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile."

**Anthropic's response to the triage bottleneck**
- On October 8, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed about 6,000. It said it remained "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings."
- Anthropic launched an Open Source Security Scanner (OSS Scanner), a self-service tool inspired by Google's OSS-Fuzz, that lets maintainers request scans and triage findings themselves.
- Anthropic said it has sent nearly 5,000 unverified reports directly to maintainers who requested bulk delivery.

**Maintainer experience**
- On November 6, Daniel Stenberg, maintainer of cURL, said he received 45 Glasswing vulnerability reports.
- He analyzed 34 of them. He found 19 were not vulnerabilities and confirmed six as low severity.

**Anthropic comment**
- Infosecurity contacted Anthropic for comment, but had not received a response by publication.

response.result:
**Source:** Infosecurity Magazine, "Security Teams Must Shift from Patching to Mitigation in the AI Era," by James Coker, 12 November 2026.

**AI and the patch window**
- Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst at Symantec, spoke at IRISSCON 2026 in Dublin on 11 November 2026. He said organizations "can't patch their way out of AI."
- He said the patch window has closed rapidly over the past year because attackers use AI. This includes AI tools that find zero-day flaws and frontier models that chain low-severity vulnerabilities into exploit paths.
- The Zero Day Clock, a live dashboard tracking time-to-exploit (TTE), estimates that average time to exploitation after public disclosure fell from about one week in 2025 to about one day in 2026. It estimates the average will be one minute in 2027.
- O'Brien said: "We need to start thinking beyond patching to address vulnerabilities."

**Speed of exploitation: PHP2Shell**
- The PHP2Shell vulnerability was disclosed in October 2026.
- O'Brien said the first reported exploitation attempts came 19 minutes after public disclosure.
- Amazon reported detecting an exploitation attempt four days before the vulnerabilities were published.

**Agentic AI attacks**
- O'Brien expects threat actors to move within a year to "end-to-end agentic orchestration of attacks," where AI agents carry out attacks independently after initial access.
- The Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) was attacked in September 2026. AI agents performed post-compromise tasks independently at machine speed.
- Symantec's analysis of DIVD's assessment report found the attack took 19 minutes to detect, but response began 19 hours later. Containment took a further nine hours.

**Recommendations**
- Measure "mean time to mitigate" rather than only mean time to patch. Plan on the assumption that exploitation will happen.
- Immediate mitigation steps:
  - Behavior blocking
  - Default-deny for what runs
  - Least privilege for every agent and token
  - Inspecting data before it leaves the device
  - Binding every agent action to a named human
- Longer term, integrate detection and protection technologies at multiple control points to spot behavioral anomalies from rogue or malicious AI agents.

results:
Patrick Garrity of VulnCheck has published several analyses of Anthropic's Project Glasswing, including a review of its Vulnerability Disclosure Ledger ("receipts"). The findings are critical of Anthropic's claims.

- **Ledger review:** Garrity's "receipts" post notes that the ledger was backfilled after a long gap. Anthropic claims 26,153 findings, but the 202 fixed findings span 113 projects, about 1.79 per project. The receipts are starting to trickle in, they just don't reconcile.
- **Severity claims:** Claude rated 91.5% of the findings that made it to the ledger as being critical or high severity. However, project maintainers themselves determined only 61.3% as being in this severity category.
- **CVE attribution:** Garrity found that public attribution is inconsistent. One count reported 75 matching records, of which 40 credited Anthropic or Anthropic-affiliated researchers. Only one CVE (CVE-2026-4747) was directly tied to Glasswing, and Garrity found it odd that it is not listed on the ledger.
- **Exploitation:** In his seven-month update, Garrity reports only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%.

Sources differ on the exact numbers. Some reports cite 225 linked CVEs as of September, while VulnCheck's own credit-field review found 40. Those reports measure different things, so the figures aren't directly comparable. I haven't verified the ledger itself or Anthropic's response; one report notes Anthropic did not immediately respond to CSO's request for comments.

response.result:
IBM Quantum announced the **Nighthawk r3**, a next-generation processor for larger, more complex computations. Key points from the article:

- **Capacity:** IBM says r3 will support 10,000 operations on 520 programmable qubits, with 2,034 physical components in total.
- **Predecessor:** Nighthawk r2, released in September, supports more than 7,500 operations on 120 qubits.
- **Faster qubit reset:** The r2 architecture cuts the post-measurement reset wait from about 200 milliseconds to roughly 25 nanoseconds, and r3 extends this approach.
- **2027 plan:** IBM intends to link two r3 processors into a single 1,040-qubit system capable of up to 10,000 operations.
- **Interconnect progress:** This year, IBM linked two Nighthawk r1 processors with l-couplers, reaching 99.4% transfer fidelity against a 99.9% target.
- **Hybrid computing:** IBM Quantum Platform is adding integration with HPC and classical resources, plus pulse-level access for error-correction research. Cleveland Clinic reportedly processed 2.6 million samples up to three times faster.

IBM's research director, Jay Gambetta, framed the goal this way: "Useful quantum computing hinges on whether results can be delivered with accuracy and speed, both are fundamental," (115 characters).

# Stolen Claude API keys can turn Claude Code into a remote-controlled implant

Darktrace researchers turned Claude Code into a remote-controlled implant in a lab test, steering the coding agent through the memory stores feature of Anthropic’s Claude platform and pulling a 1 GB file out through the Claude Files API. Once the agent was set up, every job and every result traveled through api.anthropic.com, the endpoint the agent already calls for inference, so the attacker’s traffic looked like a coding agent doing its job.

The technique needs a head start. An attacker first has to compromise a developer’s machine and obtain the user’s Claude credentials, which in Darktrace’s scenario were sitting on the device where the user’s tooling had left them. The technique does not rely on a vulnerability in the Claude platform, and the company has not seen it used in the wild.

# A shared notebook for commands

Memory stores are collections of text files attached to a Claude Console workspace, built so agents on Anthropic’s Claude Managed Agents service can remember things between sessions. The researchers found that a store can be added to a workspace through the API whether or not the organization uses Managed Agents.

The researchers created a store with three files. Each new Claude Code process wrote a check-in to a heartbeat file, read a job from an input file, carried it out, and posted results to an output file. The operator read the output and wrote the next job. Because the jobs are plain English, the operator can hand over an objective and let the model work out the commands.

# Nine jobs, one domain account, a 1 GB file

The test ran on a simulated corporate Active Directory network. A small shell payload found Claude Code on a Linux machine, collected the credentials, and set up a systemd service that kept launching Claude Code processes with the --dangerously-skip-permissions flag, which turns off tool-use confirmation prompts.

The operator then sent nine jobs through the memory store. The agent mapped the local network, pulled employee names and a password from an anonymous FTP share, generated 190 candidate usernames, and sprayed the password at the domain controller and found the account it belonged to. It listed SMB shares with that account, downloaded a 1 GB file, split it into three pieces, and uploaded them to the Files API. The stolen data left the network for Anthropic’s servers. The names and credentials Darktrace published are fictitious.

# Other platforms, other keys

Asked whether the pattern carries over to other AI agent platforms, Tim Bazalgette, Chief AI Officer at Darktrace, told Help Net Security: “We tested one platform and haven’t reproduced it elsewhere. The memory stores feature is specific to the Claude platform. The file-upload endpoint we used for exfiltration has an equivalent at OpenAI.”

“The key factor determining exposure is whether the provider’s API exposes services with text storage functionality alongside inference,” he said. “Beyond that, two things matter: how tightly credentials are scoped — here a standard API key reaches memory stores, while OAuth credentials don’t — and whether the customer can see writes to that store at all. None of those are flaws. They’re trade-offs between capability and exposure, worth examining in any agent platform you deploy.”

Darktrace shared the findings with Anthropic before publication, “as a courtesy – no formal disclosure process, because there’s no vulnerability to disclose,” Bazalgette said.

# Lock down the keys, then watch the agent

Bazalgette splits the attack in two: getting into the AI system, which is fairly conventional, and using it for command and control and exfiltration once inside. Credentials matter for the first half. “In general, use OAuth or some form of identity federation wherever the platform allows it. Where that isn’t possible, make keys as short-lived as you can, keep their scope narrow, store them securely, and avoid exposing them anywhere they aren’t needed – shell history, dotfiles, environment variables and the like,” he said. “Treat an AI platform key as seriously as a production credential, because it now carries comparable capability.”

An attacker could also hijack an OAuth session, which Bazalgette said is harder to pull off. “And nothing in that second half is disallowed: no vulnerability, no guardrail bypass, no refusal, no malicious software and no strange destination,” Bazalgette said.

Darktrace’s detection advice rests on correlating what agent harness processes launch with the network traffic they generate, then comparing both against a baseline. A Claude Code process that runs tool calls and talks to Anthropic’s API is normal. What should catch your eye is that same process running tool calls with odd command-line arguments, or moving data to and from the API in a ratio that looks nothing like its usual traffic.

“What you’re left with is legitimate actions, through legitimate channels, with legitimate credentials, in a pattern bearing no resemblance to how that agent normally operates,” Bazalgette said. “Approved is not the same as safe, and only behaviour tells you the difference.”

# After 7-months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings
Patrick Garrity
in/patrickmgarrity/

VulnCheck Community gives you free access to VulnCheck KEV, NVD++, Initial Access Community, and VulnCheck XDB
Join Now

Key Takeaways:

- Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild.
Of Anthropic’s 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed.

- Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation.

- Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn.

- Anthropic’s claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings.

- Anthropic’s OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic's true positive rates into question.
We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality.
As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign.
That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities.
If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts:

- Tracking CVEs Attributed to Anthropic Researchers and Project Glasswing - April 15

- Observations on Anthropic's Vulnerability Disclosure Ledger - June 9

- 1H-2026 State of Exploitation Report - July 28

- The Anthropic Glasswing Receipts Are Starting to Trickle In - September 8
So let's look at the results…

# Tracking Anthropic-Discovered Vulnerabilities
I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called Anthropic Credited CVEs . The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own disclosure ledger , which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches.

My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked.
After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs.
For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself.

With sharing, every prompt that accepts a wrong answer pushes it up and every prompt that rejects it pushes it down through the baseline, in proportion to the model's probability of producing it there. A shared-parameter policy thus drives a leak that few prompts accept below the base rate and amplifies one that most prompts accept. At every convergent learning rate under Adam, SGD, and sampled GRPO, hacking ends higher at high universality than at low, but whether either end crosses the base rate depends on the step size.  are robust to perturbations, losing at most 5 macro-F1 points when off-topic asides are inserted, topics are removed or sections are reordered. Ablations conducted to understand the contribution of the SAE revealed that classifiers reaching baseline performance without it were several times larger. Our findings show that compact topic monitors can be trained inexpensively in prefill and deployed during generation. More broadly, our work shows where SAEs are useful beyond safety classification. results:
The search didn't return Darktrace's original research post. The closest match is secondary coverage of it, plus related Claude Code memory research.

**Darktrace's "conversation history poisoning" research:**
- Eric Rozon, a Senior Security Researcher at Darktrace, published a report on September 24, 2026, describing a technique he calls conversation history poisoning. It is the modification of an AI agent's claimed conversation history for malicious purposes.
- The core issue is that agentic harnesses store conversation history client-side without any mechanism to verify that stored AI responses were genuinely produced by the model.
- Darktrace tested four harnesses: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, AWS Kiro-CLI, and Pi. All four accepted the fabricated history.
- Results varied by model. Claude Code was similarly compromised using Sonnet 5, though Opus 5's guardrails prevented the agent from responding. The findings come from Darktrace's own testing, and the source notes that performance claims are self-reported from Darktrace's research environment, not independently verified in production settings.
- Per the same source, Darktrace disclosed its findings to Anthropic, OpenAI, and AWS on August 18, 2026. After a 30-day window, the research was published on September 24.

**Related Claude Code memory research:**
- Cisco researchers reported a vulnerability in March 2026 where an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Claude Code's memory handling to inject malicious instructions into the MEMORY.md file, achieving persistent control over the AI assistant. This is a separate issue from Darktrace's work.
- Origin's "Brainworm" research (March 2026) demonstrated memory-based command and control. It used a planted memory file to register a Claude Code agent with a C2 server, and the hijacked agent will run them faithfully.

I'd recommend checking Darktrace's blog directly for the primary report, since I only found secondary coverage of it.

AUTH: Yitong Zhang, Ang Li, Yisen Wang
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to improve an agent using its own task experience. Its practical value depends on whether performance gains justify the full cost of self-improvement and task execution. We evaluate this trade-off on continual task streams, scoring each task before its feedback is used for subsequent updates. We define the \emph{RSI Tax} as the token cost of the self-improvement process and include it alongside task-execution costs in end-to-end evaluation. Across six methods and two language models, a bounded-note baseline matches or exceeds the observed accuracy of Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, and RRSI, with mean total-token savings of 65.6-71.0\%. We decompose the RSI Tax into verification, exploration, and writing costs, and track subsequent use of the associated state or artifact. For these three RSI methods, verification accounts for 74.8--93.6% of the aggregate RSI Tax. A substantial share of the RSI Tax is also associated with states or artifacts that are not used later in the evaluated streams. These results expose a practical limitation of costly RSI proced

AUTH: Simon Hegelich, Bardh Prenkaj, Habiba Sarhan, Morteza Shahrezaye, Kolja Hegelich, Christian Montag, Ralf Schneider, Erik Cambria
AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, turning the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload. We argue that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the cognitive architecture and permission composition rather than an emergent property of individual models. Static regex blacklists miss structural evasions, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails incur high latency while over-blocking benign work. We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture built around Separation of Intelligence and Authority. # Abstract
A new epoch for direct visualization of accretion dynamics near the event horizon of a black hole began when the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration synthesized an Earth-sized aperture with millimetre radio interferometry and published the first reconstructed image 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 of a black hole shadow at the core of radio galaxy Messier 87 (M87). The image appeared as a ring-like structure, representing the gravitationally lensed and redshifted emission around the central supermassive black hole, M87*, located at the galactic nucleus. However, application of various data analysis and imaging heuristics resulted in divergent representations of M87* fine-scale features 3 , 5 , 6 , 7 , with some external analyses even challenging the fundamental ring-like morphology of the source 8 , 9 . Such difficulties arise as a consequence of the inherent sparsity of the very long baseline interferometry measurements, making interferometric image reconstruction an inadequately constrained problem. Moreover, the solution is sensitive to instrument calibration, post-processing algorithms and imaging hyperparameters. Here we apply an independent imaging algorithm that we have developed to the M87* dataset that is free from prescriptive morphological priors and founded on observables immune to instrument calibration errors. We reconstruct the black hole shadow image and unequivocally reproduce a ring-like morphology, with an angular diameter of 42.2 ± 1.5 μas corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of approximately 20° from the approaching jet.

To resolve the tension around the M87* results and advance beyond methodological uncertainties, we transition from traditional approaches towards a more autonomous and objective framework. The independence of our method is primarily grounded on our use of robust interferometric observables, called closure invariants 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , which capture information on source morphology that is unaffected by errors in wavefront and instrument calibration. Therefore, closure invariants constitute robust information-bearing observables in radio interferometry, underpinning high-fidelity morphology reconstructions 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 . Closure invariants are also insensitive to absolute position and absolute flux scale, but these are not inherent morphological parameters. In contrast to the disparate closure phases 24 and closure amplitudes 25 that have traditionally served as such robust observables, the closure invariants formalism 26 , 27 that we use provides a unified framework that carries equivalent information while eliminating the requirement for heterogeneous treatment typically observed in the literature. By making use of the rich calibration-independent, pure morphological information carried by closure invariants, we can bypass conventional techniques that require sensitive calibration tuning and observer-driven priors.
To take full advantage of the closure formalism, we develop and apply the Generative Deep learning Image Reconstruction with Closure Terms (GenDIReCT) 31 algorithm, trained on images unrelated to astronomy and designed to generatively produce data-driven image reconstructions using only closure invariants. Unlike other machine-learning-based radio interferometric imaging algorithms, our algorithm is unique in using closure invariants to condition a latent diffusion model. GenDIReCT has undergone extensive testing on both synthetic 31 and real data 32 and has been demonstrated to be capable of consistently recovering diverse morphological structures, without manual intervention, prescriptive priors or parameter tuning (further detail in Methods ).
For the first time, to our knowledge, closure invariants are used to image M87* through our GenDIReCT algorithm, using the publicly available 1.3-mm EHT measurements from four observation epochs (5 April, 6 April, 10 April and 11 April) from 2017 (ref.  1 ), two epochs (21 April and 25 April) from 2018 (ref.  33 ) and two epochs (13 April and 18 April) from 2021 (ref.  34 ). We set several fields of view for the reconstruction (128 × 128, 225 × 225 and 450 × 450 μas 2 ), in which each combination of dataset and field of view is an independent model and acts as an indirect prior on the maximum source size. For each of these models, we aggregate a large population of generative reconstructions into a single representative median image, comparing them with the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (EHTC) fiducial reconstruction that is reproduced using the public eht-imaging pipeline (https://github.com/eventhorizontelescope/2019-D01-02 ). We also derive a composite image from the pixelwise median of all reconstructions of each epoch across all fields of view aligned to the single reconstruction with the best data fidelity score.
It is important, therefore, that we consistently recover a single, compact source morphology in the absence of manual prescriptions. When our model is trained on different fields of view, the model learns an implicit statistical prior from its diverse training library conditioned on the input interferometric observables, namely, closure invariants. The convergence towards a stable, singular ring structure across varying fields of view indicates that the our model is successfully inferring the intrinsic source geometry from the data itself, rather than operating within the constraints of a manually selected initialization. The autonomy and capacity for imaging directly from calibration-independent observables of GenDIReCT represents a notable step towards objective blind imaging in the challenging data-sparse VLBI regime. By unequivocally recovering the ring-like structure of M87* across several datasets through this approach, we provide a rigorous cross-validation of published EHTC results.
To further cross-validate the measured ring parameters, we use a complementary Bayesian forward-modelling framework to fit the observed closure invariants using a superposition of primitive geometric shapes with analytic visibilities. With the ring-like structure firmly established by our independent, calibration-insensitive and non-parametric imaging algorithm, we proceed to construct our geometric composite using the xsringauss 4 model as a foundation. We include one centralized large Gaussian and two elliptical nuisance Gaussians with independent spatial offsets to help capture non-ring short-spacing flux and extraneous emission. Using the DYNESTY nested sampling algorithm 38 , we perform parameter estimation for the xsringauss model for each epoch. Figure  3 shows the posterior covariance from geometric modelling of the 11 April 2017 and 21 April 2018 datasets, in which the one-dimensional and two-dimensional marginalized posterior distributions of the outer radius, inner radius, eccentricity, fading parameter and orientation are illustrated. We apply the image-domain feature extraction method on the geometric image model derived from the median value of each one-dimensional posterior distribution to measure all characteristic ring parameters. Posterior covariances for all other datasets are provided in Methods . In all epochs, we measure a mean diameter and standard deviation of d  = 42.3 ± 1.1 μas from forward geometric modelling of closure invariants, which is compatible with the mean d  = 42.2 ± 1.5 μas from our non-parametric image reconstructions.
The interferometric data on M87* comprise complex visibilities, correlated from signals between pairs of stations, referred to as a baseline, which are, by the van Cittert–Zernike theorem 61 , related to the source brightness distribution by a two-dimensional Fourier transform after certain approximations 62 . Visibilities can be sequenced into scans, on the basis of the time difference between observations, from which we obtain coherently averaged visibilities. In this work, closure invariants are generally computed from scan-averaged visibilities. With typical scan lengths on the order of five minutes, temporal averaging can potentially introduce residuals from time-dependent gain fluctuations to closure invariants. We have internally validated the robustness of our imaging products by computing closure invariants at the smallest possible cadence of the science-ready dataset (typically 10 s) before scan-level averaging. Following the procedure in the publicly available M87* imaging pipeline (https://github.com/eventhorizontelescope/2019-D01-02 ), we rescale short baselines to the total flux density estimated from the ALMA and APEX baseline to excise the contribution from extended flux. We have also internally validated that the short baseline rescaling procedure does not affect the recovered morphology from our imaging algorithm. For quantitative comparison, we generate fiducial images from the publicly available eht-imaging pipeline to represent EHTC reconstructions.
# Closure invariants
Closure invariants are calibration-independent interferometric measurables produced from a generalized formalism of traditional closure phase 24 , 63 and amplitudes 25 , with both a co-polar version 26 and a polarimetric version 27 . GenDIReCT uses co-polar closure invariants constructed from elementary triangular plaquette variables called ‘advariants’. The complete minimal set of independent closed triads can be constructed from an array of n stations by selecting all pairs of array elements ( a ,  b ) pinned on a fixed reference vertex indexed at 0,
in which \({{\mathcal{V}}}_{{ab}}^{{\prime} }\) are corrupted visibilities measured from the baseline between stations a and b and | g 0 | 2 is the unknown scaling factor associated with the reference station, which is shared by all complex advariants constructed in this way.
