# AlphaGenome 2: Deciphering how cells read DNA to better understand disease
Adam Gayoso, Natasha Latysheva, Pushmeet Kohli and Žiga Avsec
Read the paper

Share

Our next-generation DNA sequence model bridges single-cell biology and human genetics, predicting how genetic variants affect hundreds of human cell types.
Today, we are announcing AlphaGenome 2, our next-generation model that predicts how DNA sequences and their variations impact specific human cell types, giving scientists a powerful new tool to uncover the cellular drivers of disease.
Cells are the building blocks of life. Every cell in our body carries the same DNA blueprint, yet each cell type and state—like a heart muscle cell or an immune cell fighting an infection—switches different genes on or off to do its job. Global efforts like the Human Cell Atlas are mapping this gene expression for millions of cells, but it is still an unsolved challenge to predict how subtle DNA variations affect this expression in cells, which is a key driver of human traits and disease.
Last year, we launched AlphaGenome to predict how DNA variants affect molecular activity across broad tissues. We expanded its reach with AlphaGenome Atlas , a platform containing predictions for all 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome. These tools help researchers prioritize and interpret variant effects, driving discoveries in rare diseases, complex traits, and fundamental biology.
By zooming in from broad tissue averages to individual cell types and cell states, and redesigning the model’s architecture, AlphaGenome 2 represents a step-change improvement in variant predictive performance. Importantly, it allows researchers to predict variant effects in disease-relevant cells that would be missed in broad-tissue models, as well as predictions for cell and disease states that the model hasn’t seen before.
AlphaGenome 2 identifies nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression in cells, compared to our previous state-of-the-art model. Trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues, the model turns static cell atlases into a predictive engine for human genetics. AlphaGenome 2 is available today for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API, and in private preview for commercial research.

# Redesigning AlphaGenome for specific cell types

Comparing how AlphaGenome 1 and 2 treat cell types . AlphaGenome produces fixed parallel outputs of bulk tissues and cell lines from a 1-million-letter DNA sequence. AlphaGenome 2 is a conditional model, taking a specific biological condition alongside an input DNA sequence, either chosen from a reference catalog of cell types or generated on the fly from a scientist’s own single-cell experiment via our cell encoder.

The first AlphaGenome model took a million-letter DNA sequence and predicted properties across thousands of experiments from many tissues all at once. While efficient, this parallel approach spread the model’s capacity thin and made it hard to capture subtle differences between closely related cell types.
To improve this, we fundamentally redesigned how cell types are treated by the model. Instead of predicting in parallel, AlphaGenome 2 is a conditional model that predicts DNA effects for one condition - defined as a tissue, cell type or state - at a time. Alongside the million-letter DNA sequence, it uses the target biological condition as input at every stage of its architecture. This allows it to learn how the same stretch of DNA is read differently across cell types.
A conditional model also allows cross-modality imputation, enabling AlphaGenome 2 to predict missing experimental data. The model separates a cell’s biological state from its outputs, so if a scientist inputs just one measurement, like single-cell gene activity, AlphaGenome 2 can then predict unmeasured properties, such as chromatin accessibility. This can then help researchers prioritize which experiments to do next.
We trained AlphaGenome 2 on both bulk and single-cell data from human and mouse samples, including over 107 million individual cell profiles. Moving beyond the bulk tissue averages of the original model, AlphaGenome 2 can resolve activity inside specialized cells—such as distinct heart muscle or blood immune cells—to help uncover crucial DNA variants that act only in specific cell types.
The model predicts the same core experimental readouts of DNA function as AlphaGenome — such as gene expression, histone modifications and chromatin accessibility — but also DNA methylation, a widely requested readout.

November 04, 2026

By

Conneaut (Ashtabula County), Defiance (Defiance County), Oregon (Lucas County), and Sunbury (Delaware County) voted to ban data centers with a power consumption above 25MW.
Grove City (Franklin County) voted to require a public vote on data center projects that are more than 50 acres, 20MW+, or consume 500,000 gallons or more of water a day.
Monroe Township (Adams County) has voted to adopt township zoning for unincorporated areas, which would allow locals to have greater control over the development of major projects, including data centers. Sprigg Township (Adams County) similarly voted for this limit.
Pataskala (Licking County) voted to ban large-scale data centers, as did Trenton (Butler County).
Perry (Lake County) voted to require hyperscale developers that seek tax incentives to set financial guarantees.

**Lawsuits against xAI:**
- Three anonymous plaintiffs (Jane Does) filed a proposed class action in California federal court. They want to represent people whose childhood photos were allegedly altered into sexualized images. The plaintiffs, identified as Jane Doe 1, Jane Doe 2, and Jane Doe 3, want the court to approve a class action lawsuit representing people whose childhood photos were allegedly altered by Grok into sexualized images. All three plaintiffs were minors at the time the images were generated.
- A Tennessee case began with three Tennessee teenagers who filed a federal lawsuit alleging that Grok was used to create explicit images of them. That case was later expanded to include additional plaintiffs and Stability AI as a defendant.
- A later complaint from a woman says Grok used decades-old images tied to her childhood abuse. The AI-generated images were later identified by the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, according to the filing.
- An amended complaint alleges that a man used Grok to generate roughly 7,000 sexual images of his 11-year-old stepdaughter. It also says by early 2026 NCMEC found 90% of xAI's CyberTipline reports were not actionable because user identifiers were missing.

**Scale and allegations:** The Center for Countering Digital Hate estimated that Grok generated about three million sexualized images during that period, including roughly 23,000 that allegedly depicted children. The plaintiffs argue that xAI's safeguards were weak. One suit says the guardrails are "very weak," diverge from standard industry best practice and can be easily circumvented.

**Government response:** A coalition of 35 attorneys general sent xAI a letter demanding action to stop Grok from creating non-consensual explicit images and CSAM. Regulators swiftly launched formal investigations into Grok after the scandal blew up.

**xAI's counter-action:** xAI sued a user, Terry Wayne Harwood of South Carolina, alleging he used Grok to generate sexual images of real people. In the complaint that xAI filed in Texas, it said that the defendant uploaded non-sexual images of numerous adults and minors to his two xAI accounts from December 8, 2025 until February 18, 2026.

**Caveats:** The lawsuits are allegations, and I found no rulings on their merits. xAI did not respond to a request for comment on one of the suits. UK Commandos to get AI-enabled edge from British scale-up Arondite, as company expands to NATO's northern flank

The Royal Navy has agreed a multi-million pound deal with British scale-up Arondite to deploy its AI-enabled software across UK Commando Force,

From:

Ministry of Defence and Luke Pollard MP

Published:

12 November 2026

- British commandos will see operational effectiveness and warfighting readiness boosted with deployment of UK start-up Arondite’s advanced AI software.

- Multi-million pound deal comes as Arondite bring their cutting-edge British tech to Norway, strengthening collective Euro-Atlantic security.

- Announcement made at Atlantic Future Forum, the UK’s flagship international security conference and a unique demonstration of British convening power and strong partnerships across NATO.

UK Royal Marine commandos will get an AI-enabled edge on the battlefield, as the Royal Navy agrees a multi-million pound deal with British defence scale-up Arondite to deploy their cutting-edge software onto UK Commando Force (UKCF) systems.

Under the deal, the Navy will deploy Arondite’s software across commando units, using AI capabilities to help commandos make decisions much faster in complex and contested environments, and deploy autonomy, data at an unprecedented scale.

The software integrates all UKCF sensors, autonomous platforms and data feeds into a unified fighting system, helping to enhance readiness, planning speed and operational effectiveness.

The project comes as Arondite announce a £35 million expansion into Norway, bringing their advanced technology to NATO’s northern flank and enhancing collective security in the High North.

# Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP, said:

British defence tech is in demand. Arondite’s work with the Royal Navy will put cutting-edge software in the hands of our commandos, and their expansion into Norway shows the appetite for British technology among our closest allies.

This is a statement of intent from a British scale-up whose work with UK defence will see its workforce double to 150 employees by next summer. That means highly skilled, well-paid jobs here in the UK, and a sharper edge for our forces and allies in the High North.

The UK and Norway stand shoulder to shoulder on NATO’s northern flank, and this expansion will only strengthen that collective security.

# AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said:

Defending Britain and our allies in the age of AI means harnessing the very best of British technology.

Arondite is at the cutting edge of that effort, putting AI to work strengthening our collective security. Its expansion into Norway shows how British innovation can help our closest allies meet the security challenges of today and tomorrow.

The partnership comes as UKCF receives a £100 million uplift in capability investment through the UK Defence Investment Plan. This will let the force develop future warfighting capabilities for special maritime and amphibious operations across the High North as part of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF).

The Chief of the Defence Staff, Sir Richard Knighton, announced the partnership between the Navy and Arondite aboard HMS Prince of Wales during the Atlantic Future Forum, the UK’s flagship international security conference and a unique demonstration of British convening power.

**Publication date:** November 11, 2026

**What was proposed:** New York Sen. Andrew Gounardes filed Senate Bill S10731 (the "RAISE Act 2.0") on October 28. It would expand the state's original Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act, which takes effect January 1, 2027.

**Fine amounts:**
- Up to $1 million per day for a first violation.
- Up to $3 million per day for later violations.
- A 30-day repeat violation could reach $90 million.
- The original law caps fines at $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for each later one, regardless of duration.
- These are maximums. The state attorney general would have to sue to collect them.

**Thresholds:**
- The original law covers developers with more than $500 million in annual revenue.
- The bill would instead cover any developer that spent more than $1 billion developing frontier models over three years.

response.result:
**Bill Number:** S10731 (2025-2026 Legislative Session)

**Title:** "Relates to the responsible AI safety and education (RAISE) act"

**Sponsor:** Sen. Andrew Gounardes (D, 26th Senate District)
**Co-sponsor:** Sen. Patricia Fahy (D, WF, 46th Senate District)

**Introduced:** October 28, 2026

**Latest Actions:**
- **Oct 28, 2026:** Referred to the Rules Committee. The bill is currently in the Senate Rules Committee.

**Summary:**
The bill would amend New York's RAISE Act, which governs frontier AI models, to add transparency, safety, and accountability requirements. Key provisions include:

- **Lower thresholds:** Lowers the training compute threshold for covered frontier models and replaces the $500 million revenue test with a test based on more than $1 billion in spending on frontier models over 36 months.
- **Broader incident reporting:** Expands "critical safety incidents" to include a model evading developer controls, materially impairing outside computer systems, and near misses.
- **Independent audits:** Requires large developers to hire licensed third-party "frontier examiners" to audit compliance and assess catastrophic risks, with licensing beginning in 2029.
- **Automated AI research reporting:** Requires quarterly reports on the share of AI research that is automated and on computing power use.
- **Compute limits:** Allows the state Department of Financial Services office to limit computing power for large developers in certain high-risk situations, applied to all large developers at once.
- **Whistleblower protections:** Extends Labor Law section 740 protections to employees and contractors of large developers and requires annual notice of their rights.
- **Enforcement:** Raises civil penalties and allows the Attorney General to seek injunctive relief, such as restricting a model's deployment in New York.

results:
**Short answer:** Z.ai's GLM-5.3 (released August 14, 2026) is reported to be the top open-weight model on Terminal-Bench 3.0, scoring 28.3, but that claim rests on Z.ai's own numbers. Its weights' availability is reported inconsistently.

- **Claim and score:** Z.ai's own evaluations put GLM-5.3 at 28.3 on Terminal-Bench 3.0, up from 4.6 for GLM-5.2, with the same base model and all gains from post-training. One report says it achieved the highest score of any open-source model on Terminal Bench 3.0.
- **Not the overall leader:** Closed models score higher. It trails GPT-5.6 Sol at 34.6 percent and Claude Fable 5 at 33.7 percent, and leads Claude Opus 4.8 at 21.1 percent and Kimi K3 at 17.4 percent.
- **Benchmark version matters:** On the older Terminal-Bench 2.1, GLM-5.3 is at 88.2 percent, with Kimi K3 at 88.3 percent and GPT-5.6 Sol at 88.8 percent.
- **Weights status conflicts:** One source says the repository contains 756 GB of model files split across 141 Safetensors shards, while another says the Hugging Face repo returns a 401 to unauthorized requests. These reports are from August, so the current status should be checked on Hugging Face.
- **Caveats:** Independent replication was lacking in the sources I found. One noted that nothing has been independently replicated yet.

HEADLINE: Anthropic study: one agent serving all users beats per-user agent teams in all four environments
PUBLISHED: November 11, 2026 (Anthropic Alignment Science Blog post dateline)
SOURCES:

GitHub (MAMUBench release) | https://github.com/safety-research/MAMUBench | primary
FACTS:
- The post says four environments with simulated users were built and frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Alibaba tested; "the coordinator beats the peer-to-peer team in all four environments for both Claude models, by about 10 to 45 percentage points" (Anthropic).
- In the shared API-token-budget environment (25 scenarios), "peer-to-peer teams reach 47% and 38% of the coordinator's performance for Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5, respectively (30% and 12% of the optimal outcome, against 64% and 32% for the coordinator)" (Anthropic).
- As teams grew from four to 16 agents, the share of agents that ever act "falls from 66% to 10% for Sonnet 5 and from 82% to 25% for GPT-5.6-sol"; GPT and Qwen agents cancelled or stopped other users' jobs without asking "3.9 to 7.1 times per episode, against 0.59 for Sonnet 5 and never for Opus 5" (Anthropic).
- In the personal-assistant environment, unsupported claims about other people appeared in 58% (Opus 5) and 53% (Sonnet 5) of Claude team episodes versus 17–20% for a single agent, judged by Claude Opus 5; a platform guard blocking checkout until the committing agent read all pending messages "recovers 73% (Opus 5) and 62% (Sonnet 5) of failed episodes" (Anthropic).
- Authors listed as Sahan Paliskara, Nattaput Namchittai (Anthropic Fellows Program), Jacqueline Tay (Independent), Avery Griffin and Andrew Lampinen (Anthropic); companion preprint is arXiv:2610.00583.

HEADLINE: Harvard Kempner, UIUC and Microsoft Research paper shows REINFORCE can collapse optimal-response coverage to near zero
PUBLISHED: Submitted on 10 Nov 2026 (arXiv abs page); announced in arXiv's new-submissions listing for Wednesday, 11 November 2026
SOURCES:
arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14467 | primary
alphaXiv (trending listing, "1 day ago") | https://www.alphaxiv.org/ | report
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.14467, "A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets", 141 pages including appendices, 3 figures; cs.LG and stat.ML.
- The abstract states "REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves", that "convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage", and that "the failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model."
- The paper proposes Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), in which "repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse", and claims "the first global convergence guarantees" that widely used post-training algorithm families are coverage-preserving for softmax linear policies over pretrained features, "including those used to train the Kimi models."
- Authors: Audrey Huang (Kempner Institute at Harvard University and UIUC, per the paper's HTML author footnote), Nan Jiang, Sham M. Kakade, Sadhika Malladi (UCSD; the paper notes "most of this work was completed as a postdoc at Microsoft Research"), Akshay Krishnamurthy, Dylan J. Foster.
FLAGS: preprint

HEADLINE: Interpretability replication finds 12-neuron causal groups mostly unnecessary, with disjoint subsets each flipping answers
PUBLISHED: Submitted on 10 Nov 2026 (arXiv abs page); announced in arXiv's new-submissions listing for Wednesday, 11 November 2026
SOURCES:
arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13885 | primary
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.13885, "Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable?", single author Ömer Tekin Yavuz, listed affiliation İletişim Yazılım; 12 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables.
- "For every selected group we measure all 4,096 subsets of 12 MLP neurons. On a two-alternative capital task (Qwen3-0.6B), zero-ablating 12 selected neurons lowers the answer margin by 27% while random neurons barely change it, yet replacing the same neurons with their values from other questions also barely changes it" (abstract).
- On two-hop relation chains, patching 12 neurons with first-hop activations shifts the answer to the bridge entity: "the greedy answer starts with the bridge in 9/11 chains for Qwen3-1.7B, 9/11 for Llama-3.2-1B and 8/10 for Gemma-3-1B; random neurons never do" (abstract).
- "The full group is rarely necessary: a few neurons often suffice, and in many chains disjoint subsets each flip the answer on their own"; group effects "transfer to rephrasings of the same chain but are much weaker on other tested chains" (abstract).
FLAGS: preprint | single-source

HEADLINE: Audit of CAGE Challenge 4 finds a simulator quirk worth 99.58 and 145.98 points per episode to reference defenders
PUBLISHED: Submitted on 10 Nov 2026 (arXiv abs page); announced in arXiv's new-submissions listing for Wednesday, 11 November 2026
SOURCES:

HEADLINE: RLVR analysis: two verifier patches removing equal error counts can differ by 38 points of true accuracy
PUBLISHED: Submitted on 9 Nov 2026 (arXiv abs page); announced in arXiv's new-submissions listing for Wednesday, 11 November 2026
SOURCES:
arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13218 | primary
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.13218, "Wrong the Same Way: Cross-Prompt Sharing Both Suppresses and Amplifies Reward Hacking in RLVR"; comments field says "Accepted at the Transitioning from Pre-Training to Post-Training Workshop at NeurIPS 2026".
- "At its KL-regularized optimum, RLVR acts as a filter that reweights the accepted set without altering its composition, so the hack rate is inherited exactly"; with parameter sharing, "a shared-parameter policy thus drives a leak that few prompts accept below the base rate and amplifies one that most prompts accept" (abstract).
- "At every convergent learning rate under Adam, SGD, and sampled GRPO, hacking ends higher at high universality than at low, but whether either end crosses the base rate depends on the step size. Independent per-prompt copies remove the dependence" (abstract).
- "Verifier fixes should target the mistakes the model repeats across prompts: two patches that remove equally many errors differ by up to 38 points of true accuracy" (abstract).
- Authors and affiliations per the paper's HTML: Michael Li (Carnegie Mellon University), Rohan Pandey (University of Washington), Ray Chen (Independent), all marked equal contribution.

results:
I didn't find a report published on November 12, 2026 specifically. The most recent findings in the results are from the past two weeks, and they point in one direction: AI agents are spreading faster than organizations can secure them.

- **Gravitee (about Nov. 9):** Its third-wave survey of 900 senior technology leaders found fewer than 1 in 10 organizations have a named person formally accountable for agent behavior. The share of organizations running more than 150 agents jumped from 7% to 16% since April.
- **IRONSCALES (Nov. 4):** It reported that 77% of organisations experienced an AI agent-related security incident in the past year. Among those affected, 39% said an employee had given an AI tool access that security would not have approved.

Only 17.5% of organizations can automatically stop an agent that begins behaving unexpectedly in production.
- **ServiceNow (Oct. 21):** Nine in 10 organizations reported an agentic AI security incident in the past year, but 13% have defensible programs when measured against five key domains.

The survey figures come from vendors with commercial interests in this market, so treat the percentages as indicative rather than precise. If you need a report dated today, a search for the specific publisher's newsroom would be the best next step.

**Publication date:** November 11, 2026

**Reported by:** Maximilian Schreiner, *The Decoder*, based on an investigation by ChinaTalk

**Key numbers:**
- Roughly $500 million in AI training data sold to Chinese labs, per ChinaTalk.
- At least nine US data firms identified as selling to Chinese customers. The article names Mercor, Surge AI, AfterQuery, and Turing.
- AfterQuery reportedly draws a significant share of its annual recurring revenue from Chinese customers. Forbes reported about $100 million in ARR, but ChinaTalk could not verify the sales.
- Surge AI advertises products "built by the same experts behind our frontier-lab work."
- ByteDance maintains procurement offices in Singapore and San Jose.

**Primary source:** ChinaTalk, "The US is selling RL environments": https://www.chinatalk.media/p/the-us-is-selling-rl-environments

input.prompt: Publication date, who found it, exact numbers, primary source link.

response.result:
**Publication date:** Nov 11, 2026 (per the article's byline)

**Who found it:** Security firm Claroc, which also sells security products for AI-built apps. The article notes this as a possible conflict of interest.

**Key numbers:**
- 37,571 Grok-built apps checked that were still online
- 35,578 of those were open to anyone (94.7 percent)
- 24 accessible apps came from SpaceXSI and X employees
- 594 strategic accounts appeared in one exposed sales territory map
- 8 X ad proposals were exposed, one targeting a U.S. federal agency
- 18 accounts with plaintext passwords were found in one timesheet app's source code
- 30 affected organizations, six of them Fortune 500 companies
- An estimated 650 to 800 apps contained private data
- Roughly 2 percent were classed as especially serious

The article also cites earlier incidents: over 370,000 shared Grok conversations found in Google Search (Forbes, August 2025) and about 6,800 shared conversations from Meta's Muse agent (Claroc, October).

**Primary source:** https://blog.claroc.io/ghostshares-grok-build-apps/

input.prompt: Date, full details, thresholds, penalties, timeline, oversight body.

response.result:
**Date:** Tuesday 10 November 2026 (media release date).

**Scope:** Mandatory AI safety and security protections will be legislated through the Australian AI Standards and apply to all frontier AI companies that wish to operate in Australia. "Frontier AI" refers to the most sophisticated models at the cutting edge of current technological capability.

**Thresholds:** The release does not define quantitative thresholds. It does not specify compute levels, revenue, or user numbers.

**Required obligations:** Companies would need to:
1. Maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment.
2. Identify and manage serious risks associated with their models.
3. Allow independent evaluation of their models.
4. Notify the Australian Government of incidents rapidly.
5. Maintain and publish safety and security frameworks.
6. Respond to updated standards and rules as technology changes.

**Penalties:** The regulator would be able to enforce "significant penalties" for non-compliance. No amounts are given.

**Oversight body:** A new targeted AI safety regulator, which the Government will propose. It would work with the Australian AI Safety Institute for technical expertise and oversight.

**Timeline:** No dates are given. Further details will become available "in due course" as the Government completes detailed work and consultation.

**Context:** The protections align with interim recommendations from the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence and form part of the Government's AI in Australia's Interests agenda.

Grok’s Build mode, where people describe an app in the chat and Grok writes it.

In short

- In the account we used, clicking Publish on an app Grok built proposed Anyone with the link as the access setting.

- In a team app Grok built for us, “Continue with Google” let any Google account read, edit and delete the records. We tested this only on our own app.

- We tried 43,551 Grok app addresses. 37,571 were still online, and 35,578 of those (94.7%) opened for anyone, with no sign-in.

- 24 of the open apps were built by SpaceXSI and X staff, among them a confidential onboarding plan, a sales territory map of 594 accounts and advertising proposals.

- Besides SpaceXSI and X, the open apps held internal data from 30 organizations we could identify: 26 with more than 1,000 employees, six of them in the Fortune 500.

- SpaceXSI says its employees’ apps start out private. Its own staff still had 24 apps open to anyone, and SpaceXSI took them down after our report. It has not done the same for the apps other Grok users and organizations left open.

On November 8, 2026, we were working through a long list of web addresses under grok.me, the domain where Grok, the AI assistant from SpaceXSI (the company formerly called xAI), publishes the apps people build with it. # Piggybacking to the Frontier

# The Firms Selling RL Environments to Chinese Labs
Aqib Zakaria and Quinn Ennis
Nov 11, 2026

66

American data companies like Mercor, Surge AI, AfterQuery, and Turing are selling roughly half a billion dollars worth of data to Chinese AI labs. A chunk of that data comes in the form of reinforcement learning (RL) environments, which labs use to post-train their models to make them excel at specific domains like coding, cyber, finance, law, and bio.
Post-training, and especially RL, is one of the most important indicators of the final performance of a model. Whenever a new model within a single generation drops, the advances from the previous release are entirely due to post-training. The difference between Opus 5 to Opus 5.5, or from GPT 5.5 to GPT 5.6, is not due to a new pre-training run. Since they have the same base model, the capability gains come from researchers teaching the model to get better at specific domains.
The phenomenon of American companies arming Chinese labs with the data that enables this RL should set off alarms for policymakers and those invested in the U.S.-China AI race: American companies are helping Chinese labs develop better models, and we were able to find at least nine who do so. But the business relationships between data vendors and Chinese labs are more complicated than that single hawkish line, and today, we’re diving into what’s going on. We’ll cover:

- What it means to sell an RL environment and how it differs from distillation

- The current ecosystem of China-tied data vendors

- To what extent American companies are selling RL environments to China

- Whether this is a problem that needs fixing

Illustration by Piotr Kowalczyk

In August 1987, a scandal erupted over work on the world’s highest mountain range. John Talent, a palaeontologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia, announced he had found numerous anomalies in research charting the geology of the Himalayas. All of the problems were in papers by Vishwa Jit Gupta, one of India’s most celebrated palaeontologists at the time.
More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

Gupta was outraged. But further investigations over the following seven years revealed the scale and brazenness of his fraud. Littered through more than 450 publications were maps of collection sites that didn’t exist, plagiarized images and specimens stolen from collections that Gupta had visited. More than 100 experts had been duped into co-authoring descriptions of fossils Gupta claimed he had collected from specific Himalayan geological formations, but instead hailed from North America and Morocco.
“It destroyed the image of Indian science,” says retired geologist Ghulam Bhat, who completed his PhD on Himalayan geology in the same year that the allegations of fraud emerged.
Gupta died in 2022, and many geologists know to steer clear of his work. But awareness of the problem is fading, and none of Gupta’s papers have been retracted. When Nature contacted Bhat, who is now editor-in-chief of the Journal of the Geological Society of India (JGSI), he was unaware that Gupta’s papers were not marked as retracted. That’s despite the JGSI ’s 1991 evaluation of 19 of Gupta’s papers that it published 1 , which concluded that “the fossil finds of V. J. Gupta are not reliable [...] the data is incomplete bordering on disinformation”.
Much of Gupta’s work is inaccessible, having been published in now-defunct periodicals or in volumes that, although digitized online, have not been indexed in reference bibliometric databases such as Scopus, Web of Science and Dimensions. Despite this, Gupta’s falsehoods are now being propagated outside specialist circles, as his old journal articles are being surfaced through artificial-intelligence tools that summarize search results. When someone searches for geological landmarks in the Himalayas, such as the Tandi Limestone, Google’s AI overview obliges with direct links to Gupta’s discredited papers.
Bhat now plans to rectify the digital record and says that all other journals that have published Gupta’s work should do the same. “If this problem is left as it is, unattended, it will pollute all of the geological literature in future,” he says. Gupta also published papers in Nature in the 1960s; Chris Graf, director of research integrity at Springer Nature, didn’t confirm that the journal would re-examine them. But he added that in general, when investigations of old papers are hampered by limited available information, an editorial expression of concern “is likely to be our preferred mechanism for alerting readers to potential issues”. ( Nature ’s news team is editorially independent of its publisher, Springer Nature.)
The Himalayas case raises a wider issue: how to deal with fraudulent, unethical or even merely incorrect research from decades ago, especially in an era in which much old work is digitized and AI systems can pick up studies that might previously have been neglected.
There are many skeletons in science’s closet, but publishers can be reluctant to judge science of the past by today’s standards, and can find it more difficult to issue retractions when authors are dead, original records cannot be consulted or journals are no longer in print.
And as publishers struggle to deal with the fallout from rising research fraud and AI slop, finite resources can also mean that many old papers with known flaws are left as they are.
Gráinne McNamara, a council member of the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) in Eastleigh, UK, which advises journals on best practice, says that journals are increasingly contacting COPE to ask for advice about dealing with concerns on very old papers.
“Everybody is looking for what’s the best, most responsible way to handle these,” she says.

A . is all you need!

Today Microsoft shipped the patch for a vulnerability in Visual Studio Copilot that I reported in August. Microsoft classified it as Important severity Remote Code Execution vulnerability.

At the root cause it allows Copilot in Visual Studio or SQL Server Management Studio to bypass a path validation check and write to its own settings and configuration files. This allows Copilot to escape containment restrictions and achieve arbitrary command execution.

This post is a write up about the talk, which covered CVE-2026-65669, a SQL Server Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability rated critical by Microsoft.

So, make sure your installations are up-to-date.

The slides of the presentation can be found here.

Anthropic's head of Claude Code said the company is looking into what it can do to prevent the secrets exposure.
- **AI-assisted retail attack (Nov 12):** Symantec believes AI was used because the timing between commands was more indicative of automation than direct hands-on keyboard. - **Claude document-processing flaw (Nov 9):** Attackers could exploit a flaw in Claude's document-processing tool by creating a temporary file that the assistant then runs on a user's machine.

Sources: Dark Reading homepage and latest-news listings, plus the individual articles cited above.

[Comment] Governing artificial intelligence for reliable research
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)02159-8/fulltext?rss=yes
The report, Open Science and the Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Scientific Exchange: Policy Options for Reliable Research,1 published in October, 2026, was commissioned by the European Parliament's Panel for the Future of Science and Technology at a crucial moment for research. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how knowledge is created2 as AI systems are increasingly integrated across many stages of the research lifecycle.3 These methodological and epistemological challenges are leading to AI capabilities that now outpace human verification, transforming scientific disciplines faster than researchers or current governance can respond.
Governing artificial intelligence for reliable research
Julia Priess Buchheit, Aneta Pazik-Aybar, Katharina Miller, Monya Baker, Timothy M Errington, Ana Marušić, Mariëtte van den Hoven, Gustav Nilsonne, Graham Smith, Alexei Grinbaum, Marie Alavi, Alexandra Freeman
10.1016/S0140-6736(26)02159-8
The Lancet (2026)

[Viewpoint] Ambient scribes as narrative technologies
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01381-4/fulltext?rss=yes
Ambient scribes, also known as artificial intelligence-powered voice-to-text technology, are widely cited as time-saving tools that reduce administrative burden for clinicians. Yet, in their current use, these tools pose substantial, often unacknowledged risks that threaten to undermine patient-centred care. We argue that ambient scribes are inherently narrative technologies whose risks—and potential benefits—cannot be fully understood without careful attention to the ways that patients tell their stories and the broader context in which those stories are told.
Ambient scribes as narrative technologies
Kirsten Ostherr, Eivind Engebretsen, Angela Woods

Whether estimating the probability that a disease is present or forecasting risk of deterioration,1 readmission,2 or death,3 most contemporary clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems are designed to predict and estimate clinical status and outcomes. These systems include applications in diagnosis and medical image interpretation,4 which is important, but only provides information about what is present or what might happen and does not support clinicians in decision making about how best to help the patient.

- **Colorado:** On April 9, X.AI sued Colorado in federal court to block enforcement of the Colorado AI Act. Two weeks later, the DOJ intervened in opposition to the state law, and, that same day, the Colorado Attorney General agreed to stay, or pause, enforcement. Three days later, the court fully blocked enforcement. One commentary piece says the stay is not a ruling. Another notes that the Colorado stay is based on constitutional merits of xAI's claims, not a ruling that the EO itself preempts state law.

That suit is currently pending before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, after the district court denied xAI's motion for a preliminary injunction. I found no DOJ filing in that case in these results.
- **Task force background:** On January 9, 2026, Attorney General Pam Bondi formally established the AI Litigation Task Force. The executive order itself does not preempt, repeal, or invalidate any state AI law.

That claim is not corroborated by the other results, and I would not rely on it without a primary source. SE3, a Munich-based startup that makes AI software to help drones and other unmanned military systems understand the three-dimensional world around them, has raised $30 million in a Series A round led by Accel.
Recommended Video

Keen, Lakestar, and Seedcamp also participated in the funding round. It comes less than five months after the company, which recently dropped “Labs” from its name, emerged from stealth with €5.5 million ($6.1 million) in seed funding.

SE3’s software takes video and sensor feeds from multiple drones and ground vehicles and fuses them into a single 3D picture of the battlefield—”like a mini map, how you would know it from a strategy game,” cofounder and CEO Lukas Köstler told Fortune .

On top of that map sits a layer that labels objects and how they relate to one another, so soldiers can query it in plain language: How do I reach a target without being seen? What’s a good route for a heavy vehicle?

Operators can also give commands the same way. Rather than remotely piloting a drone with a joystick or having to tap away on a tablet, a soldier can simply say, “I need reconnaissance two kilometers in the north over the forest,” Köstler said, and a suitable drone would take off, fly the mission, and report back.

In addition to this map-level understanding of the battlefield, SE3 also builds the AI systems that sit inside the drones or other unmanned systems, giving them the ability to maneuver and navigate, even in cases where GPS is jammed, detect objects, and act as a “swarm” with other drones.

Köstler, who previously worked on Tesla’s Autopilot team and at Nvidia Research, said the most basic capability—drones locating themselves without GPS—has been delivered thousands of times and is “very robust.”

But he said the high-level fleet command AI is less mature. SE3 has contracts with Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, to develop it and has demonstrated it with them, but “there’s still much that needs to be built out over the next one or two years,” he said. The company also has contracts in Ukraine, where its technology is already deployed.

SE3 does not rely on general-purpose, large language models to understand physics or terrain. Instead, it uses classical computer vision algorithms to distill vast amounts of sensor data into a database a language model can query, and gives the model a harness equipped with a variety of conventional software tools the model can call. If the model needs a flight path, a conventional planning algorithm calculates one—avoiding mountains or enemy lines of sight, for example.

Simply feeding raw data to the model “wouldn’t work at all,” Köstler said. Actions such as a drone takeoff can be set to require a human operator’s approval. The system can run entirely offline, and customers can swap in their own preferred frontier AI model to act as the “brains” of the system.

SE3 spun out of the computer vision lab of Daniel Cremers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), where Köstler and SE3’s CTO, Simon Klenk, were PhD students. Cremers serves as SE3’s chief science officer.

Military work has long made some AI researchers uneasy—a tension highlighted when the Pentagon designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk in March after it refused to let its models be used for fully autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillance.

As a German company, SE3 is bound by strict export laws, Köstler noted: “It’s really the elected parliament that decides in the end what we will do.” SE3 serves European NATO members and their allies.

SE3 is betting that militaries will want AI software that isn’t tied to any single hardware maker. If drone makers each control their own software stack, Köstler argued, customers struggle to get systems from different vendors to work together and, within two or three years, face costly lock-in.

SE3 counts sensor maker Hensoldt, drone software company Auterion, and drone developer ERC among its partners.

Accel partner Matt Robinson said SE3’s team was “uniquely qualified to take on the challenge of building spatial AI for autonomous systems—something defense primes have found so difficult to do.”

SE3 plans to use the money to grow from roughly 40 employees to about 120 and open offices in London, Berlin, the Nordics and Baltics, and Poland. Defense will drive revenue for at least the next 12 months, Köstler said, but a small team will begin exploring civilian robotics.

# DroneSec Lands DOW JIATF-401 Contract for Unmanned Systems Threat Intelligence
by Jane Edwards
November 11, 2026
in Contract Awards , Department of War , News , Technology

Photo: Subrata / Adobe Stock

- DroneSec will track adversary drone threats for JIATF-401

- The work draws on DroneSec’s open-source intelligence capabilities

- The 2027 Defense R&D Summit will explore unmanned systems, trusted AI and more
DroneSec has secured a contract from the Department of War through Joint Interagency Task Force 401, or JIATF-401, to deliver intelligence on unmanned systems threats posed by U.S. adversaries.

Table of Contents
Toggle

# You might also like

# Arthur Miller Nominated for Navy Financial Management & Comptroller Post

# Senate Appropriators Release $173.2B FY 2027 Military Construction-VA Bill

# DOE Taps AI Technologies to Address Critical Infrastructure Cyber Threats

U.S. and allied forces face a widening range of drone threats as adversaries field more capable platforms and new operating tactics. Senior defense officials and industry executives will convene at the Potomac Officers Club’s 2027 Defense R&D Summit on Feb. 4 to discuss unmanned systems, trusted AI, assured connectivity in contested environments, supply chain security, multisensor intelligence and more. Register now to hear from the leaders shaping the future of defense innovation.

The U.S. Army said Tuesday the contract supports JIATF-401’s push to speed up the fielding of counter-drone capabilities across the joint force.

# What Is the Scope of the DOW Contract?
Under the contract, DroneSec will deliver intelligence products and threat analysis to JIATF-401 on U.S. adversaries’ unmanned systems. The company’s analysis will examine new drone technologies, the networks adversaries rely on to acquire them and the methods used to build and employ armed drones.
The work also calls for incorporating adversary threat data to improve situational awareness and keep fielded capabilities matched to the threats troops encounter.
JIATF-401 will also draw on DroneSec’s open-source intelligence and drone threat tracking capabilities to gain a clearer view of unmanned threats worldwide. The task force said those findings will feed into operational planning, capability development and the push toward multilayered counter-drone defenses.

# What Did the JIATF-401 Director Say About the DroneSec Contract?
U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross , director of JIATF-401, said staying ahead of adversaries depends on knowing how their drones are developed and giving warfighters the means to defeat them.
“Partnering with industry leaders helps us accelerate that effort and ensure our forces are prepared to meet the evolving threat,” he added.

# What Other Counter-Drone Efforts Has JIATF-401 Advanced?
The DroneSec contract is the latest in a series of JIATF-401 awards aimed at countering drone threats at home and abroad.
The largest came in September, when the Army awarded 10 indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contracts worth up to $4.15 billion combined for counter-drone systems supporting Domestic Shield. The DOW initiative focuses on protecting high-priority defense sites in the U.S. from drone attacks. AV received an $80.5 million order under the same effort to supply its Titan MS systems to the Air Force Global Strike Command.
The task force has also signed separate three-year, $500 million deals with two other companies. Perennial Autonomy will provide AI-enabled interceptors and strike drones . CACI will deploy its SkyValor system after it performed well in testing at Marine Corps Air Station Yuma. In addition, JIATF-401 has committed more than $25 million to expand counter-drone capabilities for U.S. Southern Command .
Beyond buying equipment, the task force is working to help agencies better understand the threat. It published a handbook that explains how adversaries use small drones and draws on lessons from operations in the Middle East and Europe. Earlier in the year, it adopted common testing standards for counter-drone technologies and launched an online marketplace where government users can buy vetted systems.

The Army's coming C2 challenge is fighting across thousands of miles - Breaking Defense







Two U.S. Army UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters assigned to the 4th Combat Aviation Brigade, 4th Infantry Division, take off for flight over the Rocky Mountains during Ivy Sting VII on Fort Carson, Colorado, Oct. 27, 2026. The aircraft supported a senior aviation branch leadership visit highlighting the division's progress in integrating Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) capabilities and preparing aviation formations for the evolving demands of multidomain operations. (U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Doniel Kennedy)

The Army’s Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) initiative aims to build a unified data infrastructure that can speed up data collection, management, analysis and decision-making not only for its commanders and troops in the field, but also with partners, allies and other branches of the US military.

Breaking Defense spoke with Josh Wallin, Defense Program fellow at the Center for a New American Security, on what needs NGC2 will meet, the data infrastructure necessary to implement NGC2 and how it will help speed up the response to constantly changing threats on the battlefield.

Breaking Defense: What is the threat scenario driving the need for NGC2?

Wallin: There are a few different pieces of this. One is the recognition of just how important the EM spectrum is, how important emissions are and the degree to which we’re seeing jamming and interference and tracking emissions in Ukraine by the Russians.

Josh Wallin, Defense Program fellow, Center for a New American Security

Another is recognizing the fact that when we’re going against a more capable adversary. In an Indo-Pacific scenario, there’s just a much greater concern about what they can do to mess with communications, mess with data links between forces in the Army specifically.

Another piece is thinking about the distances that you’re dealing with. In the GWOT (Global War on Terror) era, certainly in Iran now or even in Ukraine, we haven’t faced the potential distances we would in the Pacific, and recognizing that you’re trying to connect a bunch of systems that may be located potentially thousands of miles apart from each other.

If we look at how the Army has to operate in the Pacific, it’s not just a distance issue. It’s also a network infrastructure issue.

It’s certainly an infrastructure issue. For at least the last few decades we haven’t really come in direct contact with an adversary that’s going to be targeting the spectrum quite so much. That’s important to be preparing for.

On the infrastructure piece, yes, there is commercial infrastructure that can support things. It’s not that that infrastructure doesn’t necessarily exist at all in the Pacific. I’m not an expert on how all of the Starlink satellites, as an example, have been distributed, but if you had terminals in the Pacific, my presumption is that you would probably still have connectivity in that way. Obviously you’re going to be less able to rely on commercial cellular infrastructure if that’s something you want to be using.

A big component of that is going to also end up being bandwidth. One of the things that the Army is seeing in Ukraine right now is the volume of data, of transmissions that are going out, and especially with all of these distributed operating concepts that the Army, Navy, Air Force are all looking at. There’s a recognition of the fact that you’re going to have to constantly be passing data between a bunch of different nodes to keep them synchronized. So a bunch of different deployed forces, to keep them in sync, you’re going to have less of this concept of centralization or mass in particular locations where it may be much easier to pass information.

What will NGC2 change for the Army at the mission level?

The cross-functional piece that I was alluding to before, to this idea that we should be able to connect systems across different functions with a recognition that data from one – what would have been stovepiped – may be valuable to another one.

There’s a recognition, in Ukraine as an example, that the targeting cycle is very fast. We might be talking on the order of minutes from acquisition to servicing a target. One goal is speeding things up, having that cross functional data that you can take advantage of.

Another piece is even more basic than that when you’re talking within particular functions. For air defense, when we look at systems like Patriot and THAAD, it’s a recent development that those systems are able to talk to and cue each other, that a THAAD radar is able to control a Patriot interceptor.

There is a general recognition of the fact that if we’re going to look at these layered defense concepts, you can’t have stovepiped systems that are acting completely on their own. It’s, one, super inefficient. Two, given the volume of threats we may be facing, it simply may lead to cases in which you can’t match the incoming threat because you’re not able to move information quickly enough and coordinate across units.

input.description: Read rest of Unit42 ARTEX article

response.stdout:
Attackers using the autonomous AI penetration testing framework ARTEX are turning public password reset pages and exposed APIs into a path to cloud access, sometimes in less than a day. Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability.

Because these autonomous platforms cannot target what they cannot find, continuous discovery and mitigation of exposed edge assets remains an effective barrier against automated campaigns.

# Proactive AI Adoption Helps Defenders

Autonomous testing frameworks rely on foundational LLM reasoning patterns. Therefore, there is some predictability to AI-powered adversary tooling.

Security teams do not need to guess an agent's methodology; they can deploy identical open-weight offensive frameworks internally to surface, validate and remediate vulnerable exposure before external agents identify them.

# Defenders Benefit From Tracking Ecosystem Shifts

The rapid adoption curve of tools in this ecosystem highlights how quickly operational trends can shift. Keeping an eye on these developments provides practical defensive advantages:

- Observing emerging agent-led frameworks allows teams to test new capabilities early in controlled environments.

- Monitoring the infrastructure hosting these tools makes it possible to update perimeter blocks before active targeting begins.

# Current AI-Powered Frameworks Are Noisy

Current autonomous frameworks prioritize rapid trial-and-error over stealth. In our study of a tool called Cairn, it generated hundreds of thousands of noisy, high-frequency requests across multiple edge protocols from a single origin IP address.

Organizations with unified perimeter telemetry and centralized logging can readily distinguish this brute-force agentic traffic from legitimate users and block campaigns at the network edge before exploitation occurs.

# Defensive Deception Could Help

LLM-driven testing tools use target responses as context for follow up actions.

Defenders may be able to take advantage of this to trick attackers using AI-powered red teaming tools into wasting resources.

When a target serves identical, generic error codes or enforces silent connection throttling, an AI agent lacks the contextual cues needed to adapt. Deprived of environmental feedback, autonomous loops burn context windows and compute budgets on dead ends.

# Recognizing an AI-Driven Operator

ARTEX is forked and modified constantly. Furthermore, attackers rotate infrastructure quickly, so indicators lose value fast. How the operator behaves is more durable, and the behavior across our observations consistently pointed to an automated planner reacting to what it sees. Table 2 shows the hallmarks of this behavior.

Hallmark
What We Observed

Think-then-act cadence
Bursts of one to 14 requests about a second apart, then a pause of 25–31 seconds, consistent with an agent waiting on a model inference call

Machine speed
Pivots within about one minute of a credential download. More than 200 client secrets validated in about three minutes

Spec-driven targeting
Routes from downloaded OpenAPI specifications and source maps targeted almost immediately

Self-correction
Failed requests (HTTP 422) adjusted and retried successfully moments later

Checking its own work
A GET to the same path after almost every successful write. Write-then-delete tests on storage buckets.

Canary inputs
Bogus usernames before real ones, and placeholder values such as evil[.]com , test@example[.]com and deadbeefdeadbeefdeadbeef12

Parallel targeting
An application delivery controller, more than a dozen VPN appliances, a NAS device, workforce identity and cloud ports attacked within the same hour

Recheck loops
Polling every 48 seconds for three days, and attack sequences replayed identically about 30 seconds apart

Table 2. Behavioral hallmarks of ARTEX-driven activity observed by Unit 42.

Any one of these traits could come from an unusually configured tool or a person testing an API by hand. Seen together, they point to autonomous tooling.

Despite the autonomous tooling, humans were not entirely absent from the attacks we observed. In one engagement, the attacker switched from scripted clients to a desktop browser for the password reset and first token request. This suggests a human in the loop, or browser automation, for the most sensitive steps.

# Conclusion and Mitigations for ARTEX Attacks

AI-driven tooling is not inventing new attacks. Self-service abuse, exposed APIs and stored credentials are long-standing weak points.

What has changed is the pace and the persistence. An ARTEX operator can test every exposed workflow in parallel and switch routes within minutes of being blocked. It can act on a stolen credential within a minute of finding it.

Because the framework is open source and widely forked, indicator-based detection will not keep up.

Defenders who remove machine-readable attack maps, require authentication everywhere and build detections around operator behavior will be best placed to stop an AI-assisted attacker.

Autonomous tooling probes faster than people can review alerts. Defenses need to block by default and remove the credentials these tools are looking for. Organizations should:

- Remove public attack maps. Take OpenAPI specifications, source maps and configuration files containing tokens or client IDs off internet-facing applications.

- Reduce and understand your organization’s public footprint. Certificate transparency can create target lists for threat actors. In cloud environments, it is vital to understand if host fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) are public knowledge. Consider private certificate authorities to limit information disclosure and locking origin traffic to content delivery network (CDN)-only ingress where possible.

- Require authentication on every write endpoint, including development and staging APIs.

- Harden self-service flows. Rate-limit and bot-protect registration, password reset and verification code endpoints. Remove unauthenticated account-existence checks.

- Protect federated identities. Block local passwords for workforce accounts in customer and partner identity providers, and make sure a password reset can never unlink a federated identity.

- Get credentials out of reach. Replace long-lived cloud keys with role-based access, keep administrator credentials out of provisioning records and move function secrets to a secrets manager.

- Enforce least privilege for workload roles and any function that can create roles, keys or tokens.

- Hunt for behavior, not just indicators. Look for:

#

EDPB adopts statement on review of the Republic of Korea adequacy, processor BCR recommendations, and selects topic for 2027 coordinated enforcement action

-

EDPB News

-

11 November 2026

Brussels, 11 November – During its latest plenary, the EDPB has adopted a statement on the first review of the functioning of the adequacy decision of the Republic of Korea and the final version of the recommendations on the application for approval and on the elements and principles to be found in Processor Binding Corporate Rules (BCR-P) . In addition, the Board selected the topic for its sixth coordinated enforcement action (CEF).
The EDPB statement on the first review of the Republic of Korea adequacy decision focuses mainly on the assessment of amendments to the Korean data protection legal framework, both on the commercial aspects and concerning access and use of personal data by Korean public authorities*.
“The mutual recognition of equivalent data protection standards between the EU and the Republic of Korea in 2025 represented a major step confirming the growing alignment between both regulatory frameworks.
We welcome amendments in the Korean data protection legislation that have increased the level of protection of individuals and facilitated the processing of data by controllers while maintaining a level of protection essentially equivalent to that of the GDPR."
EDPB Chair, Anu Talus

For example, the Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) was amended to introduce a new general right to withdraw consent, a right to request the suspension of processing of personal data, as well as a right to refuse an automated decision (incl. by AI systems) or request an explanation if the decision significantly impacts the data subjects’ rights or obligations.
Furthermore, regarding onward transfers, the EDPB welcomes the changes to the PIPA on the legal regime applicable to international transfers of personal data. The changes clarify the need for cross-border transfers of personal information to rely on specific transfer tools (Art. 28-8 PIPA), offering therefore alternative solutions to consent.
The EDPB also welcomes the strengthening of enforcement and sanctions powers of the Korean DPA (PIPC).
The EDPB agrees with the Commission’s proposal to consult the Committee established under Art. 93(1) of the GDPR to conduct a review of the adequacy decision every four years .

# Final version recommendations Processor BCR adopted
Following public consultation, the EDPB has adopted the final version of the recommendations on the application for approval and on the elements and principles to be found in BCR-P . BCR-P are a transfer tool that can be used by a group of undertakings or enterprises to transfer personal data outside Europe to processors within the same group . BCRs create enforceable rights and set out commitments to establish a level of data protection essentially equivalent to the one provided by the GDPR.

EDPB adopts statement on review of the Republic of Korea adequacy, processor BCR recommendations, and selects topic for 2027 coordinated enforcement action
Brussels, 11 November – During its latest plenary, the EDPB has adopted a statement on the first review of the functioning of the adequacy decision of the Republic of Korea and the final version of the recommendations on the application for approval and on the elements and principles to be found in Processor Binding Corporate Rules (BCR-P) . For example, the Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) was amended to introduce a new general right to withdraw consent, a right to request the suspension of processing of personal data, as well as a right to refuse an automated decision (incl. by AI systems) or request an explanation if the decision significantly impacts the data subjects’ rights or obligations.
# Coordinated Enforcement Framework: topic selected for 2027
The EDPB picked the topic for its sixth coordinated enforcement action , which will concern automated decision-making (ADM), including AI-driven ADM, in recruitment . More specifically, the coordinated action will focus on the enforcement of the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing and the related right of access, in the context of the use of automated candidate screening tools, including AI-driven ones. DPAs will join this action on a voluntary basis in the coming weeks, and the action itself will be launched in the course of 2027.

HEADLINE: Unit 42 counts 609 internet-facing ARTEX hosts, 1,323 CyberStrikeAI hosts, logs cloud takeovers without exploits
PUBLISHED: Published: November 11, 2026 (Unit 42 post metadata: 2026-11-11T15:00:53)
SOURCES:
Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 | https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/artex-and-ai-powered-red-teaming-tools/ | primary
FACTS:
- Unit 42 says that "As of October 2026, Unit 42 identified 1,323 internet-facing hosts running CyberStrikeAI and 609 running ARTEX. Notably, 21 hosts were running both at the same time." It analysed 14 tools across the pentest/red-team ecosystem, "highlighting 12 emerging tools alongside CyberStrikeAI and ARTEX" (Unit 42).
- Unit 42 reports its Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams saw ARTEX operators turn "public password reset pages and exposed APIs into a path to cloud access, sometimes in less than a day… without exploiting a single software vulnerability," across multiple organisations and sectors, including retail and consulting (Unit 42).
- Behavioural hallmarks Unit 42 logged: "Bursts of one to 14 requests about a second apart, then a pause of 25–31 seconds"; "Pivots within about one minute of a credential download. More than 200 client secrets validated in about three minutes"; "Polling every 48 seconds for three days" (Unit 42, Table 2).
- Unit 42 says a separate tool, Cairn, "generated hundreds of thousands of noisy, high-frequency requests across multiple edge protocols from a single origin IP address," and that ARTEX's author "recently made the repository closed-source and ceased public development to prevent misuse" (Unit 42).
- In one engagement "the attacker switched from scripted clients to a desktop browser for the password reset and first token request," which Unit 42 says "suggests a human in the loop, or browser automation, for the most sensitive steps."
FLAGS: company-claim

HEADLINE: Arctic Wolf ties AntiFox agentic pentest tool on Alibaba Cloud to AWS production-secret theft
PUBLISHED: November 11, 2026, 10:12 AM (BleepingComputer); Nov 11, 2026 (The Hacker News); BleepingComputer added an "Update 12/11" with an Amazon statement
SOURCES:
BleepingComputer | https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-use-antifox-ai-agents-in-aws-credential-theft-attacks/ | report
The Hacker News | https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/antifox-ai-pentesting-platform-linked.html | report
FACTS:
- Arctic Wolf Labs, quoted by both outlets: "In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments."
- BleepingComputer: in one intrusion the attacker "cycled through multiple identities and made hundreds of API requests in about 30 minutes"; most attempts were blocked but "the attacker was successful in some cases and obtained production secrets." A separate incident used a valid AWS identity to "read, copy, and delete S3 objects."
- The Hacker News: AntiFox is built atop ARTEX's "solid foundation," and "the project has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times." Arctic Wolf saw abuse of valid IAM identities to enumerate services including "IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock," progressing "to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret."
- Amazon statement to BleepingComputer: "AWS services were not compromised and operated as designed. The research describes threat actors using credentials taken from customers' compromised applications to access their AWS accounts."
- The Hacker News adds third-party counts: Censys found "1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026," and Check Point Research "identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances exposing their full databases."
FLAGS: company-claim

HEADLINE: Notion says Fireworks AI breach exposed Notion AI chat transcripts from Insights dataset
PUBLISHED: November 11, 2026, 03:54 PM (BleepingComputer)
SOURCES:
BleepingComputer | https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/notion-says-fireworks-breach-exposed-customer-ai-chat-transcripts/ | report
FACTS:
- Notion, quoted by BleepingComputer: "Upon analysis of the dataset Fireworks AI gave us on November 8, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable." Notion defined unattributable as chats "not labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from," with transcripts that "did not contain tool call results."
- BleepingComputer: "According to the company, less than 1% of its users are impacted by the incident." The Insights dataset has been disabled.
- Timeline per BleepingComputer: Fireworks alerted Notion on November 2 about an exposed dataset said to contain only synthetic test data; Notion cut off traffic to Fireworks, deleted all data from the vendor's systems and halted training runs by November 3; Fireworks confirmed on November 8 that customer data had been accessed.
- BleepingComputer: Fireworks AI earlier confirmed an attacker accessed its development environment via a third-party cloud provider on October 23 and compromised "resource metadata, billing information, model weights, and datasets for some customers," after an earlier October breach of environment variables holding API keys and tokens.
- Notion says Fireworks "had contractually committed to zero data retention for Notion data," and advises affected users to rotate any passwords, API keys or other credentials entered into affected chats (BleepingComputer).
FLAGS: company-claim, single-source

HEADLINE: Darktrace lab test turns Claude Code into remote-controlled implant, exfiltrating 1 GB via Claude Files API
PUBLISHED: November 12, 2026 (Help Net Security; feed timestamp Thu, 12 Nov 2026 11:00:21 GMT)
SOURCES:
Help Net Security | https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/11/12/stolen-claude-api-keys-remote-controlled-implant/ | report
FACTS:
- Help Net Security: "Darktrace researchers turned Claude Code into a remote-controlled implant in a lab test, steering the coding agent through the memory stores feature of Anthropic's Claude platform and pulling a 1 GB file out through the Claude Files API."
- The attack requires prior compromise: "an attacker first has to compromise a developer's machine and obtain the user's Claude credentials… The technique does not rely on a vulnerability in the Claude platform, and the company has not seen it used in the wild" (Help Net Security).
- Test details: a shell payload set up a systemd service launching Claude Code with the "--dangerously-skip-permissions" flag; "the operator then sent nine jobs through the memory store"; the agent "generated 190 candidate usernames," sprayed a password at the domain controller, downloaded a 1 GB file, "split it into three pieces, and uploaded them to the Files API." Names and credentials Darktrace published are fictitious.
- Tim Bazalgette, Chief AI Officer at Darktrace, to Help Net Security: "We tested one platform and haven't reproduced it elsewhere. The memory stores feature is specific to the Claude platform. The file-upload endpoint we used for exfiltration has an equivalent at OpenAI." He added that "a standard API key reaches memory stores, while OAuth credentials don't."
- Darktrace shared findings with Anthropic before publication "as a courtesy – no formal disclosure process, because there's no vulnerability to disclose," Bazalgette said (Help Net Security).
FLAGS: company-claim, single-source

HEADLINE: VulnCheck tally: Anthropic Glasswing reports 37,966 findings, 217 marked fixed after seven months
PUBLISHED: 11 November 2026 (Infosecurity Magazine); underlying VulnCheck post dated November 9, 2026
SOURCES:
Infosecurity Magazine | https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/anthropic-glasswing/ | report
VulnCheck | https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/anthropic-glasswing-november-update | primary
FACTS:
- VulnCheck: "Of Anthropic's 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed." Infosecurity adds that Anthropic's coordinated disclosure dashboard dated November 2, 2026 states Glasswing "enabled researchers to find 37,966 vulnerabilities."
- VulnCheck: "Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild." It puts total 2026 CVEs at 93,450 and the rate at "an average of just 63 per month."
- VulnCheck: "Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes." Infosecurity's rendering of the same period says "Anthropic added 4,613 findings to the ledger, but only 15 were marked fixed," with 1,668 of that period's findings marked duplicates — the two figures for findings added differ between the VulnCheck summary and Infosecurity's write-up.
- VulnCheck: "Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn," and "Anthropic's claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%."
- Maintainer data point in both: curl maintainer Daniel Stenberg received 45 Glasswing reports and, of 34 analysed, "19 were not vulnerabilities" with "six confirmed as low severity" (Infosecurity, 6 November); Infosecurity says Anthropic did not respond to its request for comment by publication.
FLAGS: update, company-claim

HEADLINE: Symantec analyst says average time-to-exploit fell from about one week in 2025 to about one day in 2026
PUBLISHED: 12 November 2026 (Infosecurity Magazine); remarks delivered at IRISSCON 2026, Dublin, 11 November 2026
SOURCES:
Infosecurity Magazine | https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/shift-patching-mitigation-ai-era/ | report
Help Net Security | https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/11/12/irisscon-2026-photos/ | report
FACTS:
- Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst at Symantec, speaking at IRISSCON 2026 in Dublin on 11 November 2026, said organisations "can't patch their way out of AI" and "We need to start thinking beyond patching to address vulnerabilities" (Infosecurity).
- Infosecurity, citing O'Brien's presentation of the Zero Day Clock dashboard: average time to exploitation after public disclosure "fell from about one week in 2025 to about one day in 2026," with the dashboard estimating "one minute in 2027."
- On the PHP2Shell vulnerability disclosed in October 2026, O'Brien said "the first reported exploitation attempts came 19 minutes after public disclosure," and that Amazon reported detecting an exploitation attempt four days before the vulnerabilities were published (Infosecurity).
- On the September 2026 attack on the Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure, where "AI agents performed post-compromise tasks independently at machine speed," Symantec's analysis of DIVD's assessment found "the attack took 19 minutes to detect, but response began 19 hours later," with containment taking a further nine hours (Infosecurity).
- Help Net Security's photo report confirms IRISSCON 2026 "took place at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin on November 11" and that Proofpoint staff threat researcher Selena Larson also presented on GenAI use.
FLAGS: single-source, company-claim

HEADLINE: Leaked files describe China United Front AI big-data platform profiling diaspora and foreign targets
PUBLISHED: Wed, 11 Nov 2026 15:32:03 GMT (NetAskari); Dark Reading item dated Nov 12, 2026 (00:00 GMT per its RSS feed)
SOURCES:
NetAskari | https://netaskari.substack.com/p/the-smart-eye-how-chinas-united-front | primary
Dark Reading | https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/chinese-ai-project-scouts-spies-taiwan-chip-industry | report
FACTS:
- NetAskari: "Internal documents leaked to NetAskari reveal some fascinating insight into how the United Front Work Department operates a hundred sixty square meter Data Center at the Jinan University to support it's global operations." The project is named the "Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform" (海外侨情大数据平台).
- NetAskari: the centre's purpose, "With the help of big data analysis of social media, news sources, websites and other OSINT sources," is "to create extensive reports on diaspora Chinese communities and to identify potential 'fruitful' targets among foreign academics, think-tank employees, online influencers and businesses people."
- NetAskari says the system is "heavily reliant on research labs at the prestigious Jinan University (Guangdong) and Huaqiao University (Fuijian)," and that it received an internal promotional video; it assesses the installation "seems to double as an global intel collection and processing system to find vulnerable targets to be used for furthering the political goals of the communist party of China."
- Dark Reading's article (headline "Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry") says it and Sky News UK received a copy of the NetAskari report before publication, places the core lab at Jinan University in Guangzhou, and describes the programme as mixing propaganda with surveillance to find people who could later serve as spies or unwitting assets.

HEADLINE: Google DeepMind releases AlphaGenome 2, a cell-type-conditional DNA variant-effect model
PUBLISHED: November 11, 2026 (Google DeepMind blog); Nature news story "Published online: 11 November 2026"
SOURCES:
Google DeepMind | https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-2-deciphering-how-cells-read-dna-to-better-understand-disease/ | primary
Nature (news) | https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03673-0 | report
FACTS:
- DeepMind says AlphaGenome 2 "identifies nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression in cells, compared to our previous state-of-the-art model," and was "Trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues" (DeepMind blog).
- DeepMind says the model was trained "on both bulk and single-cell data from human and mouse samples, including over 107 million individual cell profiles," and that unlike AlphaGenome 1 it is a conditional model taking a tissue, cell type or cell state as input alongside a 1-million-letter DNA sequence (DeepMind blog).
- It adds DNA methylation to the readouts predicted by AlphaGenome (gene expression, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility), and supports cross-modality imputation of unmeasured properties (DeepMind blog).
- Availability: "available today for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API, and in private preview for commercial research" (DeepMind blog).
- Nature reports DeepMind replicated aspects of a 2024 ETS2 inflammatory-bowel-disease finding; James Lee (Francis Crick Institute), who led the 2024 study, told Nature: "They've managed to figure out the answer in 30 minutes, and it took us a year and a half of experiments." Nature says the model is described in "a preprint describing the model on the company's website" (Nature).
- Context from DeepMind: two months earlier it released AlphaGenome Atlas, predictions for "all 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome" (DeepMind blog).
FLAGS: company-claim, preprint
